Reviews.103131:
No Man's Sky is one mans vision of the ultimate space exploration game. Explore a procedurally generated universe with quintillions of planets to explore.

The updates have been coming thick and fast with a couple of massive upgrades a year. We've got multiple vehicles you can build to run around on planets with, including hover bikes and giant mechs. You can build an epic base, a farm or even a little city. You can dig into the ground or forge pillars.

Get lost in a snow storm, hide from a fire tornado in a hole in the ground, or get blown away by a tornado.

You can build your own fleet of spaceships to choose from, and command a monstrous freighter with an armada of support ships. And yeah, you can build inside that too with a mobile base you drag with you from system to system.

Every planet is really planet sized. You can roam, drive, hop and fly from pole to pole or one side to the other. If you've got weeks to spare. Or leap into space and use your drive to zoom around to the other side and land again.

You can climb mountains and volcanoes, build an underwater base and your own submarine. Find an egg to craft a real living ship of your own, and find abandoned derelict freighters in space filled with horrific things waiting to kill you.

No Mans Sky is a massively open universe to roam around in. If you want the freedom to go anywhere and do whatever you want, you might just enjoy this. And it's cross play multiplayer. So instead of exploring alone you can jump into the Nexus at any time day or night and find a community waiting to go on a wild mission with you.

I'd been somewhat following this game since a bit before launch, I'd always been interested in the concept of the game but once I heard of the really rocky launch this game had I just forgot about it for a few years. In the last year or two I'd been getting into space sim games, particularly clocking a few hundred hours in Elite Dangerous, when I realized I wasn't having fun any more with the grind in that game. It was just samey missions in samey galaxies with samey planets with samey space stations, even after Odyssey came out. I dropped the game entirely and picked up No Man's Sky on sale after hearing about how much the game has improved with updates since launch.
And holy shit, why didn't I get into it sooner. I love this game, absolutely my favorite space sim by far. I love the way they handle exploration in this game, once you get your ship up and running you can basically ignore any and all missions and just go to every planet and system you feel like, exploring and naming everything you find to your heart's content; but also, you can follow the missions to give you a clear objective on where to go and what to do at any given time.

Pros:
-Everything is procedurally generated. EVERYTHING.
-A large variety of flora and fauna: even if some of the quadrupeds look pretty similar there's a huge variety in anomalous animals- and you can claim any of them as a companion!
-Simple spaceship controls: there's a decent ceiling in skill to learn but you don't need a PHD to launch and land your ship.
-Huge planet variety: I'm still discovering new anomalous planet types, and they all wow me with the way each one is different.
-Base Building: Pretty in-depth base construction, comparable to Fallout 4's settlement creation kit- but you can build anywhere on a planet, even a portable base on your freighter!
-VR Support: It's super sick to get immersed in your headset and just gaze up at the stars on your home planet in your base.
-Constantly updating: Every few months, Hello Games drops an update that improves the game in some way. Over the last 5 years it's transformed the game from underwhelming to incredible.

Cons:
-Buggy: There's still a lot of bugs in the game, including clipping through the ground, broken textures, losing terrain changes, etc.
-Units mean nothing after a certain point: once you grind and get the best mineral farms, money is basically meaningless. That does take at least several dozen hours in my experience at least, and if you want to skip the grind entirely, it's easy to find coordinates for farms online to easily land you a few hundred million units to get a jump start.
-Hard to remap controls: The game makes you hold down a button/axis, making it nearly impossible to rebind controls to scroll wheel. There's also no in-game support to rebind VR controls, and the steam VR handling for remapping is a pain. Also, no proper left-handed mode for VR, either. It's a swap controllers or nothing type of game, so get used to aiming your multi-tool with your right hand.

In conclusion, if you like space sims, and don't care for hyper-realistic sci-fi, I highly recommend this.

Reviews.103308: No Mans Sky is a light survival space sim with a focus on exploration in an expansive galaxy. I have been playing for a few years now primarily getting into it the last two and have to say that it's charming atmosphere and endless possibility for exploration always seems to pull me back in whenever I grow bored of other titles in my library. However, as you progress and stockpile resources, and purchased goods from terminals in game most of your life support worries in game disappear, leaving the main cause of my deaths in game being gravity and an empty jet pack to be the biggest inconvenience. Exploration is fun and often exciting, whenever exploring the galaxy it can get dull finding barren nuclear environments that eat away your life support systems or barren atmosphere-less globes, it makes finding exciting planets such as fiery hell-scapes,  frozen momentous tundras, or paradise planets with perfect weather suitable for a home base to be built on. With more content such as community highlights, weekend missions with big payouts and now expeditions with limited time rewards there is always an incentive for new and returning players to come back and check out what is new. Another positive note to add is the inclusion of VR support into the game, of which I have minimal experience with but from what I have played it seems to run alright, although I still say the game is best enjoyed the classic way. To end the review I would recommend this game and look forward to future progress.

NMS is a survival game that takes place in a huge procedural galaxy, this makes for a practically unlimited number of places to explore, build on, find loot, and pick fights. My first ten hours were wondrous, and the hundred hours after that were still pretty fun.  
The alien worlds are weird in ways that I love. They range from comfortable green grassy worlds to unexplainable broken worlds, and their variety is huge! After a hundred hours, I still run across planet types that I've never seen before, complete with strange new flora and fauna. The aliens you meet are cool too, and their words give a bit of insight into the story of the universe as you learn their language.  
After a hundred hours, the game lost some charm. I can see the base animal and ship types under all the procedural generation, the planets start to look really similar, and I've read most of the NPC dialogue. The combat isn't as exciting as other games, and I never got hard into building, so I'm taking a break until the next update drops or my friends start playing again. Still highly recommend No Man's Sky for anyone who likes exploration games.

There's a lot of history behind No Man's Sky from release to where it is now, but I only played the game in its current version (starting in mid-2021), so I only have word-of-mouth to judge the game it was when it released and how far it's come.  As such, I'm not going to focus on how much better it's gotten--I don't know any of that first hand.  Instead, I'm just going to talk about the game as it is.

And the game that it is, is immensely satisfying.  The concept isn't far removed from something like Minecraft, but with the setting changed from an abstract lego-like fantasy world to a pulp-science-fiction frontier.  You're still collecting materials to survive, to construct bases, to gear yourself up to seek further and further afield, but now that exploration is met with colorful alien vistas.  

The exploration, both by starship and on foot, certainly evokes more of a science-fiction feel, but let's be clear that this doesn't play like an Elite Dangerous-style space sim.  If you're looking for more in-depth controls and combat maneuvers and sim-like flight, this game isn't going to scratch that itch, but if you live for the feeling of bee-lining to a docking bay or swooping down on an alien planet or dodging through asteroids in the rings of a planet, then it hits those notes squarely.

The collection mechanics, economy, and all of the minutiae of the game is limited in depth, but there's so much to do that you'll have spent many hours on the game before you feel like you're running out of steam.  It's not a perfect game, but it is an excellent one, and with new updates always just around the corner, it's inching its way further in quality every few months.

No Man's Sky is a vast galactic-scale exploration and building game with one of, if not [b]THE[/b] kindest multiplayer community I have ever seen in a video game. You're presented with a near-infinite galaxy (or more) of endless possibility, and how you choose to spend your time in this game is entirely up to you - and the game will not punish, but rather encourage you to find what you enjoy doing most.

I think the closest thing I can relate this to is Minecraft. Hear me out - this is a game where you can get by staying in one or two systems, never leaving, and building massive bases across your home planets to provide shelter, storage, and income via mining, hunting, and gathering. Alternatively, you can take the polar opposite approach and essentially become a nomad - exploring as many systems as you can and finding new and exciting randomly-generated planets, wildlife, and vegetation wherever you go. You can become an economy-crashing trader of resources, or a combat focused soldier who takes on sentinels in high-danger environments or hostile desolate ships. You can pour resources into making your home base a capital ship and maintaining an upgradable fleet of frigates you send out on missions to collect resources and units.

On top of this, there are 5 game modes - a relaxed Normal mode, challenging Survival mode, the obligatory Permadeath mode, Expeditions mode which are special events starting you off in specific scenarios, and of course, Creative mode to just build freely.

Now, I should mention some downsides to this game as well - the randomly generated nature of literally everything in the game makes the world feel less alive and more shallow than, say, Elite Dangerous for reference, which has dynamic politics and faction wars that can change the ownership of systems and provide more in-game lore and purpose, so to speak. Outside of the occasional scripted ship battle or when you lead a sentinel fight into space, there aren't a lot of opportunities to use your ship as a fighter. And perhaps one of the worst issues in my opinion - there are serious issues with any adjustments to the terrain of a location resetting in multiplayer if a friend or stranger visits your base. This has led to workarounds in the community as well as myself of simply building elevated bases if you intend to make them public, but it does stifle some creativity if you wish to show a friend your hard work making a big cave base in the side of a mountain, per se, and knowing you can't without it resetting.

Overall, no matter what you've heard about No Man's Sky in the past - it is a much better game now (I played it at launch and got bored after less than 2 hours). The development team behind this have released countless massive content updates, bringing what was once a shallow and pointless game up to what it is now - one of the few true sandboxes where you actually feel like you can do anything without consequence. And backing this up, as I said earlier, is the community. This community is unbelievable. In a game where it would be ridiculously easy to gun down other players without them even knowing what hit them, this community has instead chosen to always be welcoming, helpful, and just outstanding in every way. Perhaps the botched launch helped that - those seeking to play this game with ill intent got driven away believing this was a game not worth their time, which has in its wake left something much better than it otherwise could be.

Whatever the case, this game will [b]*kzrt*[/b] keep you entertained for hours upon hours on end. In my current 61 hours of playtime, there is still a limitless supply of stuff I could still do that I simply haven't yet, and that's partly due to my own relaxed playstyle of "I'll get to it when I get to it". If you [b]*kzrt*[/b] have any passing interest in space exploration, this is absolutely the game for you. It is [b]*kzrt*[/b] worth every penny.

[h1]Space Trucker[/h1]

Ovid-786 Cycler was just like any other space station in the vast expanse that was seemingly without a sky for no human, man or woman. It was almost as if it was no man's sky!

Something she rarely pondered the meaning of, most of all because this cat-eared Exosuit-wearing space farer spent her days working the trading markets between star systems. It was a lucrative business, especially if you had inside knowledge on the various demands of each economy. The crinkled and well-worn paper slotted neatly into its own Exosuit pocket told her that the galactic power industry was always in the market for engineered nano construction goods, and the smarty engineers would not get far without their holographic crankshafts or the high-capacity vector compressor provided by the industrial manufacturing colonies. And who sought something as inane as a pot of dirt? Or the hard-to-find re-latticed arc crystals? The industrial division, of course!

She had to admit, sky-hoping from one system the other did get a little confusing at times! Her sleek red and recently purchased spaceship waited patiently for her in the bays, its engine grumbling quietly at being made to idle so often.

"So, it is spark canisters , ohmic gel, experimental power fluid and a fusion core I need from here..." she murmured to herself, jabbing a hefty gloved finger at her trading route cheat sheet. The mining division would all be hacking at the dirt fruitlessly if it weren't for these much-needed supplies! And their desperation to procure these items was demonstrated in the stacks of units she would have filling her inventory at the end of each trade delivery. 

I guess, this made her a galactic trucker? 

https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2298755053

[h1]Failure to launch, but now flying high![/h1]

By now, the well worn tale of No Man's Sky's bleak launch, and Hello Game's subsequent six years of tireless updates and tweaks to bring the game to where it was promised to be, well, that is tale well known throughout gaming history! It is always worth a mention, though. No Man's Sky appears to be a labour of love, with a kind of watch-this-space feel about it. I didn't play it way back when, so I can't fully appreciate how it has come on in leaps and bounds.

BUT. I love it for what it is. But NMS offers a limitless space in which you can explore and survive. All this, and I chose to be a space trucker?! I know! Need I mention that I am also commanding a small 20 strong fleet of frigates to further explore and exploit the universe?! Whilst I sit inside my Capitol ship, sipping a glass of unnamed fluid?! 

[h1]Some other in-game time has also been spent:[/h1]

[list]
[*]Mining storm crystals from a highly volatile world. SoOoOo much monies to be made!

[*]Blowing up space pirates, and once the dust had settled, boarding said rescued ship and demanding it to be handed over as part of my reward?!

[*]Learning several new alien languages! Waay more useful than the French and Spanish I was taught at school!

[*]Finding signs of long dead civilisations, touching and MAYBE taking some artifacts, only to draw the ire of the local, meanie sentinel forces. Who then proceeded to chase me beyond the planet's atmosphere!

[*]Traded in spaceships! Now that was a side hustle if there ever was one! Picture this, you find a burning pile of junk, fix it up just enough so it can chug into the nearest space station. Then sell it at an inflated price to the unsuspecting locals! $___$=

[*]Planet hopping to try and find a profitable ball of dirt on which to make my base!

Reviews.103540:
No Man Sky is a story about how prolonged support after a failed launch can really return a game from the abyss of failure. Endless patches have began to deliver on many of the promises that were meant to be met at launch. 

That said, No Man Sky is far from perfect. The game boasts an endless universe of billions of stars thanks to the games procedural generation. Yet despite all of that, you may find yourself seeing many of the same planets again and again. You may also often find yourself wondering just what the point of all it is as you wander from samey planet to samey planet. To answer, there really isn't a point. 

That said, the game does deliver something unique and is still being supported. If you are someone that enjoys setting your own objectives and just exploring for the sake of exploring, there is still going to be something in this game to draw you in. 

The only thing the game is really missing is a creative and hand crafted touch. If the developers could find a way to work that into all of their machine algorithms, they could have themselves a masterpiece.

The one thing I will say that is huge, is that all the updates are free. I can see the game being worth easily hundreds of dollars based off all the content they have put out if they were to sell them as DLCs.

There is a lot to do. It is repetitive but there is a lot.
Exploring is the biggest asset of the game, as you explore you find research outpost, trading post, abandoned ships that you can repair and add to you collection and much more all in beautiful graphics. 
As you can expect as you move through the tiers the materials needed are more rare, although they're plenty. 
As you advance you can create your own fleet and send it on missions to bring back resource and rare items. 
Upgrade your gear, ships, and tools as you move through the tiers.
Gain reputation with the different fractions and unlock unique rewards. 
You can build your base or bases and recruit your base crew. Create a farm and harvest items. Create portals to go back and forth between your base and other planets. Build your base almost anywhere on the planets, even under water. 
Make money by harvesting, missions, trading etc then use that money to buy ships or other items.
Co-op is a little weird but some of the rewards are worth it.
All in all it is a good game. I have a lot of time on it. I usually play for a bit then take a break and come back after a few weeks to new content.

I can see how some people can get bored with gathering resources, but it doesn't take too long until you get to the point where you can just buy everything you need. I've actually logged just under 50h, so I'm not sure where the 92 hours comes from, though my kids have played an additional 4 and 7 hours respectively.

While people always talk about the huge vastness of the 2^64 planets in the game (or whatever it is), it doesn't take too long before you see "new" animals, plants, and minerals on different planets that you have already seen before, but with different names.

Great exploration, great building, great space fights (maybe too easy), and a great economy system.

However, This review will be updated once Hello Games fixes the few glitches and issues that are prevalent. I have had one game-breaking glitch where landing spawned my character on top of a building that I couldn't get off of, softlocking me and causing me to reload a save that removed a lot of progress, and there are still immersion-breaking glitches like NPC's A-posing and moving in a static manner. Animals still can be found flying in place at times too, which can break the immersion a bit.

As it stands, right now No Man's Sky is an 8 1/2 out of a possible ten for me, which will be changed as fixes come about.

Reviews.103749:
Wow, this game is immense. Compared to how it was 5 years ago, it's really changed for the better. This game could have been just like Anthem or Cyberpunk or Fallout 76; an overhyped game that came out way worse than expected and didn't get the updates it needed to thrive. And though it started that way, it didn't end that way. Hello Games could have easily taken all that money and ran, like EA or Blizzard or Bethesda. But they realized their mistake and used their resources to provide what the game needed. It went from a crappy game with barely any of the promised features, to an amazing, immense, immersive, story driven, action packed, absolutely gorgeous game.

Speaking of immense, the actual game is HUGE. There are exactly 255 different galaxies to explore, each one with billions upon billions of solar systems, all containing from 3 to 6 planets and moons. I've played this game for over 100 hours and haven't even left the first galaxy yet! That's just how massive this game is. Every human could explore this whole game for the rest of their lives, and still probably barely find every single one.

Summary Version:
This game started out shit, but got really really good. It's really really big, and you should definitely buy it if you're into games like this, or even if you're not. There's plenty to do for anyone out there.

Reviews.103811:
Okay. It's been a rocky five years, but I'm finally going to give this game the review that it does not deserve. 

Yes, I recommend it. 100% recommend it. 

This game is a solid 8/10, especially for how boring it is. And make no mistake, this game is BORING. There is only so much to do and the rinse and repeat of soaring through the cosmos to samey planets and landscapes gets very dry after a while. The environments are very beautiful, but definitely lack some much needed variation. The quests and tasks you are given also feel pointless and repetitive. Vehicle design is okay, there are some very cute combinations for ships that can randomly occur (or you can give yourself if you feel so inclined to use save editors). Speaking of very cute random combinations, you will not find that in creature design. Everything that lives in this universe (outside of the VERY cute good bois, the Gek) are either nightmarish abominations or robots. Very rarely you may run into an animal on a planet that is just goofy looking, but would be pants-soiling abhorrent to look at in real life.

I bought this game on release, played for 2.01 hours and couldn't get a refund. Years later I returned to it after seeing 100000000 articles on PCGamer about the progress it was making and decided to give it a second try. The progress was apparent, but the game was still disappointing. But I figured "Hey, focus on the things you CAN change" and I changed the way I played. Sure, I played through the ACTUALLY kind of interesting and mind bending story, but that was only so I could progress through the tech trees. But outside of that, I found myself stuck in my head single-player role-playing scenarios that were not happening in the game, but were purely set in my own imagination. When I did that, the horribly bland gameplay loop didn't matter anymore. Instead of being an "anomaly", I became the only survivor of a dead species whose planet was destroyed by the Sentinels, and my goal was to amass a giant armada comprised of all of the dominant species of the endless universe to wage an eternal war against the Sentinels and restore liberty to the countless galaxies that dot the void of space. 

No Man's Sky launched as completely wasted potential. And it still is completely wasted potential. The survival mechanics limit gameplay in ways that could be compared to being slowly suffocated with a wet pillow. The randomization of creatures should result in millions of variations, but you will see a lot of the same elements used at the same time that result in an ecosystem that looks the same. Even all the buildings look the same. No matter where you go, you are still in the same place doing the same thing, OVER AND OVER AND OVER again. But yet, I feel compelled to admit that the aesthetics of the game are pleasing. Sure, they are the same. But they look great. And to be honest, I love this game even if it has one million shortcomings. This game is boring, drab, dull, pointless, grindy, ridiculous, and bad. 

But I love it for some reason. 



TL;DR:
The game is a great sandbox. Some mechanics really hit good, others fall flat and feel as shallow as a napkin in the rain. You get out what you put in. Make the game fun how YOU see fit. Don't play this just for the story or for the aspect of "endless discovery". The game is boring, uninspired, and still to this day unfinished. 
But I like it. And I literally don't like ANYTHING.

Reviews.103894:
[h1]Things I Like[/h1]

There's just... so much to do in this game now that it's hardly recognizable as the game it once was. 

Some parts of this game are actually unsettling and horrifying. Some parts of this game are unimaginably beautiful. I've walked around on a planet that looked like something straight out of Cthulhu's sketchbook, and then walked across a planet with glittering, iridescent pink flowers that were bio-luminescent at night, while pretty bubbles floated lazily past.

The game draws you in. There is so much to explore and do, and so many different types of projects you want to try to do. I'm focusing a bit more closely on the story (not by much- it's been a whole day since I actually progressed the storyline), while my husband was off working on getting blueprints to create a truly automated farm that will collect supplies for him. I did get the ability to make a literal farm- I've got several Star Bulbs growing, because thy're pretty. Wish my main base wasn't on the radiactive ick planet, though.

I think one of my main things that I love is how quickly this game goes from unsettling horror to gorgeous exploration game. It's vast, and despite the fact that you know much of it is randomly generated, it's still incredibly beautiful. It does feel a tad lonely sometimes- big, massive planets and worlds, and not always a lot of people. It makes sense- these are whole planets in whole systems, there couldn't be enough people in the entire universe to fully fill each one- but it sometimes makes you realize just how lonely it is.

Not gonna lie, though, I think one of my favorite moments was getting a whole freaking freighter to do missions for me on its own. Freaking COOL.

[h1]Things That Could Be Better[/h1]

The game is multiplayer, but it doesn't really feel like it. My husband and I play together on a multiplayer save, and while it's nice that we're playing together, we don't really... actually play together. Every single story mission you get, you have to do separately, so if we both get a quest that asks us to build a base, we must each build a separate base- it doesn't count if I only build it, or if he does.

As the game progressed, this created this kind of duality where we both wandered off to do our own thing. We can teleport to each other's bases (sometimes, it's buggy), but it's basically non-existent that we're on the same planet, let alone the same SYSTEM as each other. The game is massive, and our story missions don't always take us to the same planet- just the same system. It's so difficult to actually stick together through the story that there's just... no point in trying. So yes, it's multiplayer, but it just... doesn't feel like it.

[h1]The Bugs[/h1]

This game is actually quite buggy. NPC's getting stuck in the floor, our characters getting launched into the sky endlessly, only to plummet back down to the ground a second later. Crashing whenever I die.

Mostly, it's pretty bearable and not a big deal. I think one of the more humorous "quirks" (not REALLY a bug) is that I set up a base on top of a spot that was used for the story, where I collected a new ship for myself. After I left, apparently the area reset itself; every time I warp back to this base, the ship I took is back again for yet another collection, and the distress beacon I found during my story quest has been reset to have a new distress message attached to it. I think I've supposedly found 15 dead pilots and their ships in this one, exact same spot. It resets every time I leave, without fail.

The saddest moment in the game for me was losing a small little settlement that had the best multi-tool I've ever seen. It was 3,400,000 credits, which I had not been anywhere NEAR for the first several hours, so I didn't bother marking it. Not fifteen freaking minutes later, I found a massive plethora of the rarest bones you could possibly find. Left the planet, got 4,400,000 credits... and couldn't find the depot. It is gone... forever.

It still hurts. I found something almost as good... but nothing will be as good as that multi-tool.

Always mark the good stuff.

Reviews.103930:
Do I think you should get this game. Yes. It's a easy game to enjoy but a hard game to love. There have been a lot of talk about the redemptive arc of the development of this game. That's all true. This is a labor of love that suffered through a mountain of outrage hurled at a very small indie team.

I recommend this game. It is probably the best laid-back space tourism game on the market. On days when I'm stressed it always makes for a very chill experience. I usually fall asleep in 30 minutes of playing it. It is beautiful and relaxing and nothing ever poses any real risk in the standard experience. I wouldn't recommend playing it any other way except creative but making it easier hardly seems needed.  This is what the designers intended and they succeeded. You have your own very chill galaxy to explore. Your own a sky with a thousand thousand thousand glittering gems to explore.

I can't stress that last paragraph enough. That's the game. That's why it's called "No Man's Sky". It's your mostly private galaxy to explore. Yes there is multiplayer. But then it's the same experience with you zoning out with friends. If you expect anything else you will be disappointed.

The game has more features, diversity, graphical fidelity and polish then ever after 5 years. It's still a mixed bag. It's best approached as an exploration game or survival game if you play it on the more difficult modes. On that level it's rewarding at first but tapers off quickly. Despite intense development the diversity on display here make planets feel the same. Doesn't help that heat/radiation/cold/toxicity are just filters and different shield bars that deplete for the players. The strategy to survive on a desert planet is the same as surviving on a frozen tundra.  Minerals and flora and fauna are noticeably diverse but you'll feel the repetition set in after a dozen planets.

Combat is clunky and easy on every difficulty level. I'd be afraid to play iron-man purely because of how chaotic combat can be. The occasional lethal glitch is also a show stopper for high risk play. I haven't seen space combat this easy since the original Wing Commander.  It's easier than that actually. Ground combat is only slightly better and still utterly uninteresting especially against the local fauna. Most times you will put up a fight for a bit and then run. And by "most times" I mean "nearly always". I think the implacable enemy is supposed to add to that "chill" nature in that you can never defeat them. You just fight them til your too bored to fight them anymore. It also makes combat feel extremely underwhelming.

Base building has some amazing work online but it's mostly despite the tools given. There just simply aren't enough options to decorate your home to your liking. Farming materials to unlock designs is also tedious and unpleasant. There are few designs for interior decoration and furniture. Interactivity with your home is minimal. You have health packs, lights, landing pads but you can't really decorate your place. So people bases are studies in clever architecture rather than interior design. In any case they are hardly worth it. You can get a larger "freighter" ship which functionally is the best base in the game and the one you will use most often. In there you just add more bland metal rooms as you need them.

After that we get into a host of small one-off systems that are all half-baked. You can train pets but they don't seem to be actually helpful or have personality. You can set up race courses but I don't see any organized way to share tracks much less organized competition.  You can create a trade routes but it's insanely easy. You don't really need to keep track of demand or supply ever. You just grab stuff at  one planet that makes widgets and instantly teleport to planet that will buy widgets. You can have your freighters collect resources and play the game for you like this was a time-gated mobile game.  None of this is any more fun then a mini-game in grand theft auto. But the diversity in game experience is welcomed to break up some really monotonous questing.

Questing even in the nexus is monotonous and rarely fun mostly because these are fetch quests where the combat is easy and nothing is hard to find after the first 20 hours. The main quest-lines are mostly not glitchy but are weird with little payoff thematically, dramatically or play-wise to recommend them.

But the tourism is first rate. Everywhere looks like everywhere else after a while which makes you feel like a seasoned worldly space-traveler or perhaps a very bleary tired travelogue writer. They even call your character "traveler" implying you should treat the game like a rootless wandering.  The universe is overwhelming but also feels small. As an artistic expression and a technical achievement I heartily approve.

[h1][i][u]THIS REVIEW CONTAINS NO SPOILERS[/u][/i][/h1]

Although it may have had a rocky launch, No Man's Sky has done nothing but improve time and time again as it's aged. After over 15 enormous updates adding heaps and heaps of new content to the game, NMS has become exactly what it was always promised to be; a beautiful, inviting, massive, experience of a game. With an incredible soundtrack backing up its amazing visuals, no paid DLC whatsoever, as well as near endless amounts of gameplay content, NMS is a triumph of developers who didn't give up on what they believed in.



[u][h1]👉👉 THE THINGS I LOVE 👈👈[/h1][/u]
My personal favorite thing about this game is honestly just the way it looks. After the most recent update (Prisms, at time of writing), the game is visually stunning top to bottom. The night skies are wide and spanning, with stars dotting the cosmos as far as the eye can see. Some planets are covered in lush grass that boasts a gorgeous bioluminescent glow that drifts in waves across the planet's surface, while others are home to enormous oceans that reflect the light of the sky back up at you. The visuals of space travel, overall design of many of the buildings and locations, ship designs, and creatures especially are breathtaking and enjoyable to see over and over again.

The variety in planets, while you may see many similar, is never-ending. You will always be able to find a new cave to explore, a new ocean to swim in, new creatures to populate them, and so much more than a single review could really cover. The amount of different ships you can obtain is plentiful, with different systems having unique ships to them. You can easily get your hands on a freighter and kick off a fleet in no time, as well as build incredible planetary bases on all sorts of different environments.

The multiplayer system is fantastically simple and allows for enormous amounts of fun with up to a 4-person party. You can all do your own missions without messing each other up, or you can do group missions super easily! You can visit each other's bases and freighters, easily trade items between friends, and so much more. Being able to simply join straight off of the Steam friend's list makes the system even easier to use, and you can bring any save file into your friend's games as well. This means you could help kickstart a new player if you have a loaded save file, start fresh with each other, or just both bring in your high-powered ships and run around like Gods!

The crafting system allows for plenty of learning, but never leaving things just totally unanswered as to "how do I do this??". If the game doesn't explain it, the incredibly well detailed wikis will! Many items that you aren't able to craft are unlocked easily by just doing quests, or for tech by buying the recipe for them, and all basic crafting recipes are explained just by simply hovering over most of the items.



[u][h1]🔥🔥 SOME MINOR GRIPES 🔥🔥[/h1][/u]
Many, if not all, of my issues with this game are largely just nitpicks more than anything else. One of the things I wish I was able to do would be build a group home base, or set another player's home base as my own with their permission to do so. Unfortunately, this sort of thing simply isn't possible in this exact way. Building your base directly adjacent to your friend's would work fine, but doesn't quite feel like a "mutual home" in the same way that having a single shared base computer would.

You cannot summon your freighter into a system that another player's freighter already occupies. While I understand the reason for this from a general gameplay perspective, it still seems kind of stupid that if I'm sitting 4 planets away, in a position where their freighter isn't even physically in eyeshot of my player, I still can't summon mine. This means that I will often have to leave to a different system just to retrieve items from my freighter, or check in on an expedition.

When it comes to character customization, we're given a large amount of color and visual options to choose between, with more that can be unlocked as you play. The same cannot be said about ships, unfortunately. Whatever you see when you purchase your ship is what it's going to stay as. No changing colors, no affixing different accessories and baubles to the exterior, nothing. Much like your exosuit, you can upgrade your ship's storage as well as install a variety of different tech to it as you wish, but that's it. Ship customization is something many players have wanted for a long time, but simply has not been added. As stated earlier, many systems have ships that are unique to that system, but these are also the only ships you will see in that system. Without potentially hours of hunting, finding the [i]exact right ship[/i] that you want may be much harder than it sounds due to the lack of ship customization.



[u][h1]✨✨ THE BOTTOM LINE ✨✨[/h1][/u]
No Man's Sky is a passion project gone better than many ever expected. After years of development by an incredibly talented team, it's become one of the most enjoyable games I can name to this day. I could talk for hours about the amount of things I've experienced in this game, and at the time of writing this I haven't even played for 100 hours yet!

[u][b]Would I recommend playing this game?[/b][/u][b]  --  [/b]Without a doubt in my mind. Absolutely, yes.
[u][b]Is No Man's Sky worth the full price tag?[/b][/u][b]  --  [/b]At launch? No. In it's current state? Wholeheartedly yes. Every penny.
[u][b]On a scale of 1-10, what would I rate this game?[/b][/u][b]  --  [/b]8.5/10, if not 9/10. If it weren't for some of the very minor gripes I have with the game, it would be a clean 10/10.

At the end of the day, No Man's Sky is an incredible experience of a game, no matter how you decide to play it. Whether you spend your days building bases, leveling mountains, discovering creatures, cataloging planets, unearthing ancient artifacts, or just flying through space and relaxing among the stars, you'll have an amazing time and want to come back for more very soon.

I notice many bad reviews for this game after its initial release. But after many critics by players and improvement by the developers over the years, this game has become a truly amazing game. You can see a wide variety of species and tons of planets to explore. Although it's not meant for combat or monster hunting in alien planets, it just felt enjoyable being able to visit planets in other star system.

Every planet has its own unique theme. It means the terrains, minerals, and wildlife would be different from one planet to another. There's an ocean planet in which 99% of it is covered in ocean. So you'll have to dive and explore interesting marine life within. There's a very cold planet which is covered in snow. And there's even a barren planet with floating mechanical objects.

You can mine minerals and wildlife for hundreds of different materials. And with them, you can craft many items or operate lots of different devices. If you're not going to use certain materials, then you can just sell them at a trading center. Or if you have enough money, just buy those materials from them. Moreover, not only can you mine on planets, but also on many other space objects which you encounter, such as asteroids or floating crystals in space. How cool is that ?

Yes it is true, that you'll see some kind of repetition here and there, but it's not that bad. They have managed to create some kind of random map generator for each planet, so you'll notice that the terrains and wildlife are adequately random and unique. So it's really a very fun experience to explore the vastness of this galaxy.

If you compare it with Elite Dangerous game, then you won't feel any grinding here. In Elite Dangerous, no matter where you are and what you do, everything seems to be grinding. In No Man's Sky, you'll be occupied with tons of different things to do, that will make you forget time. You won't notice that hours have passed already.

If you don't want to experience the trouble and time consumption of interstellar journey, then just create a teleporter on different planets, so you can jump from one planet to another instantly. That way, more activities can be done quickly between multiple star system. But if you truly want to experience the vastness of space, the radiant star light, the chunks of asteroid in planetary rings, the excitement of being in warp speed, and the thrill of entering an atmosphere, then journey with space ship is your best choice.

The developers also put some kind of missions which can be accessed in space stations. The missions are fairly varied. And although most of the game is only in single player mode or only with registered friends, the game now has minor MMO aspect. In some space station, you can really meet random players in the internet and do things together with them. I know that creating an MMO game with galactic-scale map is astonishingly difficult, but the fact that they made it, means that No Man's Sky can be one of the best Galactic-Scale MMO out there. Well at least until Star Citizen game has been fully released.

So basically this game is about 75% similar with Star Citizen. The most notable difference is basically graphic quality and planetary variation.

tldr; 'No Man's Sky' has come a long way since its release to the gaming public.  Thank you Hello Games for everything you've done to deliver to us your initial vision of this game. My time spent in the universe you've created has been fun and enjoyable. 

What a rough start 'No Man's Sky' began with.  Big, brash, bold, loud and promises of delivering a game that would make even the most cynical, hardened gamer weep tears.  Instead, those tears were of rage.

However, in my opinion the most important thing to take away is our collective tears as a community of gaming enthusiasts is what helped to provide a secondary source of fuel for Hello Games to do what I believe only two game developers, in recent memory, have done as a Mea Culpa for their respective community.  The games I'm talking about are: Final Fantasy: Realm Reborn and No Man's Sky.  The developers of each game took it in the teeth.  The fucking teeth.  And, they came back at us with something else...something better. Something meaningful.  Not just a game we would enjoy & invest hours upon hours of time into a universe they created as a work of passion.  No, not just that.  They came back to us from a place of integrity to show that the relationship between us (developer / gamer) meant something beyond just the bottom line of how much we as consumers can be nickle and dimed to death in an age micro transactions.

It's fair to say I'm not a fan boy of either of these creative endeavours.  And, I have spent more time, of the two, playing 'No Man's Sky' though not recently.  What I am a fan boy of is their respective commitment to bringing us, a fickle community of gamers (consumers), the experience we had an expectation of them presenting to us upon release.  Their word was their promise and it did not match or meet our expectation.  In time, they brought us what we wanted.

And for that, I am thankful.

I'm fine with having given Hello Games my money, and I've definitely enjoyed my 30 hours of gameplay. I've gotten a similar amount of time out of similarly priced games, so it wasn't a waste. But I was expecting to get at least a couple hundred hours out of it, which I think was a reasonable expectation; and I can already tell that's not gonna happen. So I honestly have to recommend against NMS, or at least recommend extreme caution.

The core of the problem for me is that, sure, there's stuff to do and stuff to see; but I don't feel any reason to do or see any more of it. I feel like I've finished the game. There might technically be hundreds of hours more content, but as far as I can tell it'll just be busy work. There's no challenge, no meaningful reward, and no foreseeable novelty.

You're supposed to fully explore and catalog planets, but that means spending my whole afternoon looking for gray rocks at the bottom of a lake that I must have missed. I already felt like I was getting plenty of credits and nanites, so I'd rather just save the effort, skip the 100%-scanning reward, and move on. There goes the planetary exploration mechanic.

You're then supposed to go explore other systems, but they're procedurally generated. Which means they're all slight variations of each other with slightly different combinations of stats, weather, and materials. So once you've built mini-stations on a variety of planets with the materials you want, you don't really need to keep exploring others except perhaps to find a slightly more convenient combination. So there go the system exploration and most of the flight mechanics.

Then you're supposed to mine materials from those planets, except it's more effective to teleport to the various stations you found while setting up your mini-bases and buy the materials you need in bulk. Once you've unlocked a handful of blueprints and made a few million credits from some not-particularly-rare drops, you can start crafting iridesite in bulk. Then the crafting mechanics condense down to making a couple stacks of that, teleporting to a station to sell it, buying more cobalt, teleporting back, and crafting more. You just ground away the mining mechanics. And on top of that, you don't have anything to spend the credits on anymore because you don't need a ship, protection, weapons, upgrades, or even a bigger base.

So with that you've got no reason to explore the planets, no reason to explore the systems, no reason to fly around, no reason to craft most of anything, and no reason to spend credits except to make more credits. The game encouraged me to optimize the game away, and all that's left is a to-do list that I'd only do for its own sake. I'd rather go watch TV.

So yeah, endless kudos to Hello Games for doing the right thing and completing the game at no additional cost to us. But I can't say I see the appeal of the game past my 30 hours.

Man, this game's been a ride and a half. I bought it when it was just released. It was terrible, it was complete garbage. The devs made all these promises that they didn't keep, enticing trailers with content that never existed, and this is why the game's reviews are mixed when you tally all of them up, because when the game was released first it was [b]bombarded[/b] by negative reviews en masse, for good reason.

But, somewhat reminiscent of a rare few other companies (like say Egosoft who made the X series space sims) the devs didn't just drop the game and run with the money, even if they could have, they kept developing it, they kept adding content to it, for years, and they still are to this day updating the game. There has not been a single paid dlc, all the feature updates have been entirely free, and man, this game has become good over time.

But uh, it's not perfect all right, I mean the game is great, but it's not exactly a seamless experience, most of the gameplay consist of grinding and fetch quests, alternatively it's a bit like elite dangerous, you know you have this huge galaxy to explore, a practically infinite number of planets to visit, although unlike that game (at least last time I played it) you can land on them, do stuff on them, 'make your own adventure', explore, etc, but it's ultimately going to be a repetitive experience after a point.

You can get stuck in it, like you would any good craft grinder or rpg, trying to build a cooler base, trying to make the numbers go [b]higher[/b], but it helps a lot to have a friend with you. If not just to show your stuff off and in turn seeing their stuff, then just to have some company. Sure, the game is technically an MMO right now, you're always online, you always might see another player out and about, but the universe is vast, and it's only happened to me maybe once that I encountered another player out in the galaxy at random, and even just that is astonishingly unlikely.

You can however at any point enter an anomaly, which is like a hub for players, where you can meet and interact with other players, maybe even invite one of them to a party, and there's in-game voice chat too to make the experience more pleasant (or less, depending on how you look at it).

As for the gameplay experience, if a space sim like Elite and a craftgrinding simulator like Minecraft had a baby, it would look something like this game.

(warning long review, and pretty much completely subjective, but hopefully worth a read)

Keep walking! Keep walking!
I think it's a game for a particular kind of person.   

I can honestly see why most people would pick this up and get bored within two days of owning it but personally this game invokes something in me that I can't really describe directly without pretty much giving my life story so I guess I'll do that. 

Growing up I didn't have much to do because my parents were always out working and I knew no one in my neighborhood so I was pretty lonely all the time. All I really had for a good chunk of my childhood to early teen-hood was my Xbox 360 slim and my lego sets and a lot of time by myself (also because I was never allowed outside). 

You know when you were young and you could only really muster up the courage to ask your parents to buy you a video game like once every few months? Yeah and then you'd need to play it to death so that you got your money's worth. I had to do that and I got pretty imaginative with how I'd stretch out otherwise complete single player games. 

I would boot up a game like ac4 or red dead, or some of the lego games (pirates of the caribbean, avengers) and I would just walk around in the open world and that's pretty much it. I would walk around and pretend to play out my own little story about what my characters were doing. It wasn't some intense novel-esque storytelling but it was more of just something I'd make up as I went along the world. 

Like in GTA 4 (GREAT game for a kid btw) I would follow a random npc around the map and make some silly story for why me and him needed to stick together like, for example, there was some kind of zombie apocalypse!! and the rest of the NPCS were infected and me and him needed to survive, this was all happening in my tiny little head and it was fully fledged out, I'd imagine fake dialogues, fake backstories, and even connect some of my little narratives together with regularly occuring characters in the NPCs with similar textures. It was really REALLY dumb but it was my favorite thing to do at the end of a video game and it arguably was funner for me than the actual campaign. 

When you play a game like how I did as a kid you really end up being alot more imaginative with the game's setting. To do that I think I played those games with a slower  pace. When I walked around I really looked closely at EVERYTHING because everything could be an element of my silly grand narrative and also just because I was in awe of the things I was seeing. I'd even do it on multiplayer games, cause I had no online mode or closeby friends to play with. I'd start up multiplayer maps on Halo 3 by myself and walk around and again make some funny little narrative as to why I was doing so or just straight up go sightseeing. The narrative was secondary to the looking around part I think.

In retrospect it's insane for a little kid to be doing, 
but I really would walk around at the slowest walking speed and just really pan my analogue stick around the maps,
and for a moment I'd feel like I wasn't home, 
I wasn't in my lonely room
I was a part of a large enthralling world, the scale of which being too difficult to quantify. 
A part of a world I had convinced myself  (through my imagination) to be alive but more importantly right infront of me with no limitations or rules.
like I was there with those characters in that world walking around 
and I could pretend 
that my feet felt the ground, 
and I could hear the wind brush by even though I wasn't.

 (It was so peaceful and so freeing to be able to direct myself in this world and walk to wherever I want and imagine any stories that I wanted to be happening. And that feeling was so comforting and empowering, because what I knew to be where I was, HOME, where I was stuck, was lonesome, and boring, isolating, and I couldn't see any of my friends. So having those video games to help me momentarily just be able to walk around these strange worlds of fiction that I'd forced myself into by shoehorning in my own narratives was so important to me and made me feel like I could break out of my suffocating-ly small house and into these infinite worlds.)

Now with that in mind you could imagine the insane click I had with No Man's Sky, a game built around the central gameplay pillar of walking around weird little worlds and making your own fantastic narratives and discoveries  without (for the most part) a nagging ongoing game "campaign" that obsessively curates your experience to be just like how it was intended to be played out by the game developers. 

The game was pretty much designed for the me from my childhood and it brings me right back to those memories. Me in my family's shared room infront of a blocky TV on the dusty old mattress we had under warmly colored ceiling lights that'd flicker softly when it rained, slowly walking around for hours on some random game no with no waypoints, or mainquests ( because I had finished it weeks ago), no responsibilities, and no one else around, just me and my worlds with seemingly nothing happening on screen but in my mind I was spinning and listing these elaborate webs and stories about these worlds that I knew and loved. Now put all those video games into a 10 gigabyte experience and times that experience by literally infinity and add a lot of well thought out accessibility features and you have No Man's Sky, a game that makes my experience with video game worlds as a child a real game

a warm blanket of absolute escapism.

Absolutely splendid. I first got No Man's Sky a couple of years after release, when things seemed to be improving, and it still had a lot of problems. Unless the art style alienates you, or you're expecting a good flight game (the flight model is now the poorest thing about it), I can't recommend it enough. I played Wing Commander Privateer as a kid and got sucked into Noctis in college. All I ever wanted was for someone to make a game like those – free and open and weird and janky in all the right places – and dammit, that's exactly what No Man's Sky is. You jump between frightfully compact star systems, talk to standoffish aliens, buy stuff, sell stuff, take pictures, mine, craft, soar…

The game gets a little fiddler and fancier than that, sometimes more than it needs to, but that usually doesn't overshadow the startling satisfaction of its simple core loop: Land on a planet; scan all the stuff; do whatever cool thing is in front of you; take what you need; go to the next planet. It sounds repetitive, and it is, but in the way that eating an apple is repetitive. Yes, you have to bite the apple again, but apples are for biting, and those three-legged nose birds are for scanning, so get scanning.

Or don't. Trick out your ship and run raids on cargo freighters. Build a research base by the sea. Try to learn as many alien words as you can. I've done each of things, and had great fun with them, but I always return to the pleasure of new dirt beneath my boots.

Go to a place. Check it out for a while. Cool, right? Cool.

You know, I played No Man's Sky on PS4 when it launched, and decided to pick it up again recently on PC.

Here's the rub. After playing on a save for almost 60 hours, making vast manufacturing facilities, getting an S-class freighter, and more, I'm setting up another base to mine some nitrogen. This game has been sitting in my wishlist since the date of release but thousands of negative reviews threw me off and it ended up forgotten into the void of other wishlisted games. Five years has passed and during the recent summer sale i decided to take a look into my wishlist and once again stumbled upon no man's sky. Having no knowledge of what has been going on with the game for the last five years aside from a few hearsay about the game finally redeemed itself, I decided to buy it.

What came after was waves of amazement as I flew inside my ship across numerous solar system discovering multiple planets harbouring various different fauna and flora, each with their unique shapes and forms. Not only that I found out that I could tame those animals I found, becoming my companions in my lonely journey. In the middle of all that I also managed to gather a handful of ship each with their own funcionality and design with the aim to get the perfect ship. One time I warped into an undiscoverd solar system I stumbled upon a bountiful planet Mountains, Hills, Prairies, Lakes and Oceans all roamed by animals massive and tiny, floras and minerals in every directions you faced, no dangerous storms every 5 minutes, no toxicity or radiation, and the perfect weather to live in. So. I decided to try to build a home on that planet. Ever so slowly my base grows, room by room, building by building, hallways connecting one building to another, machines by machines... And from a land with nothing but dirt and wildlife, it became a place I could call home.

I remember one event after I just arrived to one of the solar system I found myself in the middle of a battle between some pirates and a HUGE freighter, having absolutely no clue what was going on I decided to help the freighter anyway destroying the pirate's ships one by one. The battle is over. None of the pirate's ship are intact. Not long after, a communication signal was sent to my ship from the freighter inviting me onboard the freighter because the captain insist to give me a reward as a thank you gift. I board the freighter, making my way towards the control room and coming face to face with the captain. I thought I will be given some money as a reward but instead the captain offer me his title and the massive ship he commandeer. This at the time caught me off-guard because I was saving money to buy one of these, but now the game just gave it to me for free?? Well "why not?", I said to myself as I took over as the new captain.

My story above wasn't related to a main quest. I simply explore. Since the game didn't put a gun to my head forcing me to follow the main quest the moment I started a new game, I just decide to do what I want. Explore. In fact, I decided to do the main quest after I did all that. Also I CANNOT not mention how beautiful everything looks, I just love just flying around the solar system taking some beautiful screenshots of space or just flew on the planet's sky as I took more screenshots of my ship flying into the sunset.

The freedom I had while playing is what I love about the game, and yet I felt too much freedom is give to the player and not enough instructions, what I meant by that is the fact that the game started to became a bit boring after you did all of what I and another players has done. Sure the planets is different from each other, but after coming across 10 more planet, they all started to felt similar. The animals in each planets? They also becoming more and more dull. Not to mention some of the floras and minerals in each planets THEY ARE THE SAME. What about the ship?? well with 100 hours in, all of the ship in my possesion are different by type, and yet only one ship is memorable since you actually need to do some work to get it, but the rest of the ship you can just find in some random space stations in each solar system. And the base building? It's frustating, different types are hard to connect with each other. And the bugs... oh my GOD the bugs are there, I even fell inside a goddamn planet once.

And yet despite all that, I still enjoyed the game, feeling myself turns into a kid as I explore something unknown is just... wonderful.

[h1] TL;DR [/h1]
If you're looking for the perfect adventure experience filled with non-stop action and being bombarded by quests after quests uncovering more and more adventures then this game is definitely not gonna be that. But if you're looking to just enjoy yourself on a day off and take your mind off things from your life then No Man's Sky is a must try.

I waited to purchase No Man's sky, buying Elite Dangerous instead, because of the early poor reviews.  The developers really spent time on this game.  After they improved the game, I decided to give it a shot.  I use Oculus VR and I was blown away the first moments in the game.  It is beautiful, the tutorial system makes sure you won't get lost on what to do, and it offers a complete experience which ED and Star Citizen can't match. 

There is so much to the game...exploration, creativity, survival.  I am pleasantly surprised and I've only just started.  

One downside is there is no native joystick support so it takes reading a modding article and tinkering if you have an old joystick.  But...I successfully got my joystick to work eventually.   

One thing I forgot to mention, there is a bit of an RPG element to the game. The text of the story reads like an old school rpg game which I like.  Honestly I am not playing the game for the story but that it has one is pretty cool.  

Buy the game.  Especially if you have VR but even the normal game is beautiful and worthwhile.  

Could it be even better?  Yes of course.  This is not a perfect game but it is literally the best space game I've ever played and it is a great game.

Not sure where to start here, I came from Elite but they are completely different games, Elite feels like a proper simulation with gameplay tacked on the end while NMS feels like an actual game that happens to involve space travel. If you want to know what it would actually feel like to be in space I would recommend Elite, If you want engaging gameplay I would recommend NMS, the devs seem to care about your time as you can travel anywhere in a short amount of time, it feels more like an exploration game where you get to the planet you want to explore through space travel, unlike Elite which is all about travelling through space.
This is just as well as I think my biggest criticism is the flight mechanics, they are absolutely horrible and take a while to get used to. My other issue is some of the mobs are pointless to fight as they are infinite, the sentinels will respawn until you hop in your ship and wait for the timer to count down, there is also a weird creature that has eggs you can harvest worth good money early game, however you can shoot the creature and another will instantly respawn, making it pointless to fight. These are both minor irritations and overall I love this game as there is ton of things to do, the storyline does a great job of holding your hand and teaching you the basics, you have a freighter given to you after you have travelled to five systems (unlike Elite where you need to grind 5 billion for a basic freighter and then pay upkeep on it!) and you can build a huge mobile base in it as well. 
Walked to far from your ship? Then just summon it, can't be bothered to fly to your freighter? Just summon it, there are a lot of Quality of Life improvements in this game that make it a breeze to play. One of the best aspects is the community, who really don't seem to care how you play the as long as you are having fun, there are a lot of glitches and tricks to work around the gameplay if you want to go that route (plenty of you tube videos  to help out there) and people are generally ok with that, whereas Elite, while overall a great community, has a lot of people who seem to think they have the right to tell you how to play the game you paid for!!
I highly recommend as a chill exploration game where you can just have fun and do your own thing.

No Man's Sky is a faithful homage to retro science fiction of the 60s and 70s that at times encapsulates the loneliness of space, whilst offering diverse gameplay opportunities for playing with others to provide an alternative to the emotional monotony of isolation.

Soon after the insightful yet hands-off tutorial, you’ll find yourself lost amidst the countless interactable and fully explorable environments, with many worthwhile upgrades and milestones to work towards as you journey across the stars. 
Engaging story paths synergise with abstract lore elements appropriately scattered throughout the universe, and the enjoyable gameplay loops of exploration, base-building and questing allow for lore interactions and roleplay that make No Man's Sky worth more than the sum of its parts.

Most of your time will be spent exploring, and this is the game’s strongest aspect. Every single celestial body (excluding stars) is visitable, and you’ll spend much of your adventure landing on planets and moons. The thrill of sighting a far-away planet in the sky, only to fly there 5 minutes later and realise that you’re standing where you just dreamed of visiting, never wears off.

Worlds, star systems and other features that you discover are yours to name and upload. Planets range from teeming with wildlife grazing and leaping across verdant, bounding plains of fertility and lush jungle ecosystems, to icy tundras, mountainous frozen wastelands, deserts with gravity-defying rock structures and magnificent subterranean cave systems, scorching worlds ruled by hardy and dangerous creatures, to magma worlds and worlds dominated by unpredictable weather events, to redacted planets that reveal fragments of the broken simulation. It’s a science-fiction melting pot of exploration. The visuals, vistas and sceneries are breathtaking, and the culmination of updates make exploring vast alien oceans and hidden cave systems as interesting and spectacular as the worlds above.

A fleshed-out base-building system allows you to claim multiple planets as your home scattered between galaxies, as well as a portable base in your own freighter that you can summon anywhere, at any time – provided your freighter is outfitted with the required hyperdrive upgrades, that is. A huge variety of assets lets you customise your alien home to your liking, whether it be submerged in an ocean trench or overlooking the landscape along a mountaintop.

Questing provides further incentive for discovery, whether by virtue of the game’s storylines or through mission agents at space stations. These offer your basic fetch quests and “kill 10 x for 100 y” tasks, in contrast to the deeper overarching narratives that further develop the game’s atmosphere. There’s much to do, learn and discover that wouldn’t be fair to spoil here.

DLSS adds a much-needed performance bonus with little compromise in visual quality at the highest settings, but I do still notice occasional hitching. Bugs are few and far between, not including some janky gameplay elements like pop-in and weird collision effects when flying into some assets in space. Ground combat is still weak in structure and control, lacking a certain polish and intuition found in games more heavily geared towards combat; this is a small gripe for me, but worth mentioning for people who value ground combat operations. Space combat is far more polished and natural.

It's the best comeback story of the generation by far, and as a strong fan of atmospheric science-fiction, it strikes every chord for me.

A ton of stuff to do, and is hella fun to play

I'll start off with the game is fun for what it is and has a decent enough story line. I was debating between this and another game. Ultimately I decided on this because my kid is big into space and the game was multiplayer whereas the other game I was considering was not. Unfortunately I have to say the multiplayer is terrible. Friends will be playing when suddenly they drop from the "group" and after looking they were disconnected from the game fully and we are both in single player mode. This has happened repeatedly. The quest progress hangs up if all the members of your group are not in essence playing solo at times and only counts progress if you do every single piece of the quest line yourself. Initially I thought it was a good thing to force others, but the game does not give the proper prompts as if they had completed that step of the quest, but really hadn't. There are times when you get forced into multiplayer mode even though it's turned off. Systems are showing as discovered by people I've never played with (at least not intentionally). 

The graphics are pretty decent even if there's a lot of repeated artwork in the flora/fauna. Some of the sunrise/sunsets are amazing especially on ringed planets. 

There are a ton of visual bugs however, like buying the "hide electrical wiring" upgrade only to see the wiring. Also if you clear out land to build a base you may come back to have your base filled in completely. It has occurred while I was standing in my base but my friend walked out.

I'd say if you catch this on a good sale price and only want/expect to play single player then it's a good buy. Otherwise i'd say hard pass at current price and or expecting multiplayer. Maybe 2.5/5 stars on a good day.

Honestly, I've given this game so many opportunities, (even VR!) and still, I just cannot recommend it, I cannot enjoy it, I find it repetitive, boring to explore, and the worst part... INVENTORY MANAGEMENT. I really do appreciate all the effort that Hello Games has put into this game, but for me it feels like it tries to do a lot of things but none of them good enough:

-Space exploration? check. But feels like a toy space filled with MILLIONS of asteroids, I want to feel in space, not in a sea of asteroids betweejn planes that, btw, do not orbit around the star but rather just kinda orbit around themselves?? 
-Space combat? Check. probably the only decent thing of this game, but again, it's not stellar
-Space legs? Check. But planets are just repetitive... Even tho they do have stuff to do on them, some of them, it does feel like just a random mass with random stuff placed (I get it, procedurally generated, but it doesn't help with inmersion)
-FPS shooter combat? check. Probably the most auful thing appart from inventory management. It feels dull, and not smooth at all. weapons don't really feel different.
-Mining/Resource gathering? Check. It's awful. I just HATE it. Honestly, and the fact that you need to keep recharging your equipment? it's just so annoying.
-Resources/inventory management. HORRIBLE.  You have SO little space for stuff, and you need SO MUCH stuff for anything.. and Improvements take space ON YOUR ALREADY SUPER LIMITED INVENTORY!!! Honestly this alone is one of the biggest reasons I just cannot recomend this game.
-Story? Check. Cannot say much about it, but didn't feel very engaging... also most alien encounter feel exactly the same and very shallow, to not say extremely shallow.
-Building/exo/vehicles? Check. Honestly I have to say this part is preaty great. If it was not for RESOURCE MANAGEMENT AND INVENTORY. AGAIN. "just play creative man" WHY?? Why do I have to choose creative mode because the game cannot handle inventory management? I like survival, but this inventory style is plain and simple outdated.

I love NMS. I loved it on PS4, Xbox One, and now on PC. There is just so much to do and nothing that you absolutely have to do. Its a great game if you want a relaxing experience that you can play at your own pace and your own way. 

To get the most enjoyment out of it, you need to know what it is and what it isn't.

It is:
A relaxing space exploration experience
A game that lets you feel like you are creating your own galactic empire of small settlements
A game of collecting (unique ships, multitools-basically guns, frigates, discoveries, pets, etc)
A creative experience where you can build creations and name almost anything you encounter
A game that lets you upgrade most everything (a mild RPG style experience)
A game with an optional story that makes you think existentially
A resource management game
A mild action game
A game you play with friends collaboratively
A game that gives you a feeling that you are in an infinite universe

It isn't:
A space flight simulator
A competitive multiplayer game
A FPS
A game where you just shoot rocks
An epic story experience with voice acting and CGI cutscenes
A full on RPG

In total I have over 1,000 hours in this game including over 100 hrs in PCVR/PSVR and I just keep coming back to it over and over after I finish other games.

Pros: The depressive crushing loneliness that is the "main mission" is a constant attempt to throw you into a crisis of being. Requiring users to read the story was a nice touch to drive home the empty feel. the ability to build and destroy every inch of a planet is fantastic for switching up combat, survival, and base building, lending a much more 'natural' feel to structures that is sadly under utilized by the average player. The depth of every corner of the game while still retaining a simplicity that prevents things from being too "grindy" is remarkable, Nothing is ever more than a few hours away, but there is always another thing to do. The base power balance and allocation was deeply satisfying to me in a way that was previously attained by old school buildcraft using reactors to generate and recycle matter into useful tech. The food and farming remains a solid point of enjoyment with my pets always putting me in a good mood. it is tempting to log on every day just to give my little lizard cow a fresh treat and many pets.  The variety of vehicles, gear, upgrades, and tech is daunting to say the least, but with time each is very rewarding in there own right and can turn an inhospitable planet impossible to harvest into a sunday drive down the grocery store. The spike in difficulty between normal and survival is best described as "you want to enjoy your time here without much resupplying" and "Keep an eye on your resources, don't overextend" with key components like sodium and Oxygen on survival having cargo stacks of 500 units (plenty for several days of gameplay) up to normal modes several thousand (never actually filled a full stack) The community hub and ability to easily earn the premium funds gives NMS a leg up as you can always end your lone travels by joining others and showing off your fabulous new jetpack and shoulder guards.

In conclusion: NMS has many flaws and many perks that leaves you in the same mood as a family reunion, happy, sad, angry, disappointed, satisfied, glad its over, and looking forward to the next one. with only a few tweaks to variety, gameplay, and glitches this game could easily be one of the best on the market, a true underdog story i am glad to have experienced.

One of the best Sandbox/Open-World/Base Building game i've played so far.
This is a great game for people who are looking for non-competitive progression game.

You can do lot of things in this game like:
- Be an Explorer (analysing creatures, minerals, plants), exploring unlimited numbers of planets.
- Be a Space Pirate (raiding freighters to earn resources)
- Be an Archaelogist (getting ancient items like bones, metals, ornament or what not) and they spawn well on some world.
- Be a Bounty Hunter, loves doing quest? from nexus of space station you can do it. You can earn currencies like Units (money), Nanites (special currency for buying upgrades), quicksilver (mostly for customizations like decoration for buildings, character customization, jetpack customization, etc)
- Be a Builder/Gardening/Mining, loves building base and to have passive resources. Who doesn't love this stuff?
- Be a Trader, you can buy and sell resources from different solar system. You can plan trade routes on what to buy and where to sell your haul. 
- Be someone who explore scary dead ships on space with rewards to buy off, new customization.

You can follow the quest line to unlock lots of stuff. But if you prefer on your own you can do it too since you can unlock almost everything on your own via salvage data and exploration.
