I was very sceptical about this game, as it was released as a train wreck. However, the DEVs have done a great job of making it quite something. The UI still can do with a lot of work, as there are way too many clicks required and it is largely unintuitive. However, as you play, you kind of get used to it, which does not reduce the frustration by much but it makes it workable.
Refiners clearly need an overhaul. A limit of 250 stack size may be OK for a small refiner but same for a big one? It achieves nothing other than having to spend a ton of time micromanaging them.

Third thing that should not be is the map, or lack thereof. Space age with wicked technology and there is no planetary map? This is not silly, it is plain stupid. The galaxy map is OK although it is daft that you need to be in your ship and in space in order to open it. I rate it as OK because there is no means to easily find mission markers. There is still some base computer mission pending in my game and, for the life of me, I can't see where in space I have to go because had made my way towards the centre of the galaxy and covered a bit more than 100k units (UA?).

However, these three are really my main gripes, which means the game is very good by now overall.

It is a pity that you can only play expeditions during their short duration, as it means new players will lose out on content.

I can't see myself spending thousands of hours playing it, unlike Elder Scrolls, Empyrion or Egosoft's X series. However, I did get 180 hours out of it before feeling a bit bored. 180 hours is good value for money, even if you pay full price.

No Man's Sky is quite the mixed-feelings game for me.

Personally, I've put in close to 300 hours between Xbox and Steam. It is true, the game is plagued with bugs and glitches. Some bugs aren't a big deal, while others can result is a soft-lock of progress, and even death. Many of these bugs have been around for a very long time, never being addressed. That being said, many bugs have been addressed.

This game is awesome. The infinite universe concept is hard to pull off, and while NMS doesn't exactly do it perfectly, it also doesn't do a terrible job. You do tend to see a lot of the same stuff over and over, but you also find new and interesting things every now and then as well.

Base building could be better. Addressing bugs again; base building is one of the buggiest mechanics in the game. If you build a large base, there is a high chance it will all disappear over night and never come back again. Collaborative bases are the worst though, as there seems to be a syncing issue between players. If you build something, even when uploaded, there is a large chance other players won't be able to see or interact with it, even when you're online. If you decide to destroy a part of your base, there is also a large chance that portion will remain for other players, who can usually still interact with it (like it was never deleted on their screen).

The animals are alright. The huge majority of animals in NMS all eventually look like the same jumble of body parts, one way or another. This being said, there are always unique and awesome animals to be found. Companions were a great addition to the game, and with Prisms now, there is an even larger variety of awesome companions to adopt.

Multiplayer in general is very buggy. Often, both in cross play and safe-platform play, I will be disconnected randomly and often from my party (which is hugely annoying when you're trying to explore new systems and planets together).

I understand you may be confused at why my review is a recommendation after all the bashing I did in regard to the bugs in NMS. I wanted to save my overall thoughts for last, because I truly believe this game deserves a lot of love for how far it has come since launch. The game has grown so much for the best over the years, and it continues to do so now (for free!). It is certainly worth a try. It can be a ton of fun with friends, especially if you like going on adventures and finding new things with your friends. The opportunities are almost endless, especially as time goes on. Just be cautioned, you may find yourself pretty upset and bummed when one or more of these previous mentioned bugs happen to you on a regular basis.

Reviews.105443:
I can't begin to explain how much I enjoy this game, let alone, express my feelings about how it has let me feel like a kid again. 

Last night, I hopped on with 2 friends and I felt like I was in a whole new world. I battled space sentinels with my pals, traded starships, comversed with aliens, and explored foreign planets with unique and diverse creatures. At one point, we engaged sentinels and a huge walker appeared so we had to dig tunnels to hid from them. When our efforts proved fruitless, we tried to make our way back to our ships but a giant firestorm was on its way. We noticed an abandoned building and trecked towards it, all while sentinels were pursuing us and the toxic environment draining our life support. I felt like a kid, living an experience that I always dreamed of. The feeling was amazing...

We soon managed to get to our ships after the battle and flew into space, making our way towards our other friend on an icey planet. However, after we left the atmosphere, we were informed by a signal that "reinforcements" were on their way. Not knowing what that meant, we brushed it off but within moments, a MASSIVE ship, armed with turrets and a fleet of sentinels warped out of hyperdrive and we were caught up in a massive space war. We began the conflict, outmatched with our poor ships and equipment, fearing for our lives and loosing our cargo. 

Our hearts were pounding as we engaged the ships, maneuvering around space and the asteroids that surrounded us. We were outmatched so we had to get rid of the ships, one-by-one. My friends ship was heavily damaged, his shields down and hyperdrive unavailable due to being in the vicinity of the other ships. As I battled and provided backup, he managed to engage his hyperdrive and make his way towards the local spaceststion, nearly avoiding death. 

As I was left alone, stranded and helpless, I engaged in a battle I might not win but was filled with determination. I swirled around bullets, outmanuvered the ships, and barely escaped with my life, managing to engage my hyperdrive as well... 

I have put 80 hours into this game and this is the first time I have had this happen. Heck, I still haven't even finished the tutorial. 

No Man's Sky truly is an experience that I've never had before and I will continue to play it to my hearts content. Its amazing, beautiful, and blows your mind as you travel the galaxy, searching and exploring. 

I can't wait to see what comes next...

[h1] No Man's Sky is a game with a troubled past, but a bright future. Fitting for a game about spacetravel and exploration. [/h1]

Before even coming out, NMS had a troubled development with Sony pushing a small studio to the forefront of news media and raising expectations for what is, effectively, an indie game. These expectations were only made higher and higher as interviews seemingly promised more and more incredible features. Sean Murray, founder and managing director of Hello Games (who also served as one of the programmers for No Man's Sky) is many things, but a public speaker he definitely is not. Many of the "promised" features that people touted as reasons this game didn't initially deliver were never really promised in the first place, leading questions and non-answers in interviews with murray (who, if you'll seek out video interviews appeared to be very much out of his element/awkward in such a setting) lead to a lot of confusion on this front.

So, the game itself then. No man's sky admittedly did not do well on release. The game was buggy, fairly empty feeling, had no multiplayer, etc, etc. The game was a mess. Since then however, in the close to five years since initial release the game has had multiple free content updates adding in many of the "promised" features as well as plenty of other new features. For that alone the developers are to be respected.

The game itself is, as of the writing of this review, fine. Many planets feel...unfortunately empty and terrain oftentimes feels uninteresting and repetitive. The game itself still has some issues running smoothly, but that can potentially be blamed more on an outdated computer than the game itself. This being said, ultimately the game itself is still fairly fun in my opinion. Exploring the galaxy in my ship, occasionally finding something unique and new, it's relaxing to say the least.

Is the game for everyone? Probably not. Is it worth at least giving a chance? I'd say yes.

Five years after an infamous release I finally picked this one up for the first time. It's clear what the consensus is - the game has improved massively since its initial release.
The game is centered around exploration and base building. The exploration is quite interesting for the first few dozen hours as you see so many different types of planets and remain amused with the diversity and infinite procedural generation. 
Base building is another highlight of the game. Once you find a beautiful, safe planet that's to your liking you can really dig in and the game has enough to let your creativity shine if you want it to.
The storyline is okay, and the storymode is more about familiarizing you with the game than anything else.
The rest of the game is full of little add-ons that unfortunately always feel like add-ons - starfighter battles, fleet management, exocraft, upgrading everything and pets. While each have something that will gain your initial interest, it seems like you always hit some wall of progression where there's not much to do except grind for minor improvements. They all seem to lack some long-term potential. 
For example, the exocraft in this game are beautiful with great physics yet there's just not much to do except wander around terrain where you quickly get the hang of everything you can possibly bump into. Driving the two-wheeler exocraft up and down mountains is fun - the physics are almost worthy of their own game - yet there aren't really any goals or points of interest to keep you entertained. You could take on the daunting task of building a race course and trying to attract other players - but you probably won't.
All in all it's worth trying out but the lack of depth in some areas keep it short of being the epic open world game we were all waiting for.

Reviews.105753:
If you're like me and saw the Internet Historian video on this game and thought you'd give it a shot...well...maybe don't.   

The experience below is based on 5+ hours daily for about 3 weeks.

It's likely much much better than debut, but it's still not very good.  Not even for the "sale" price of $30.

Maybe if you jumped on early, you went through all the patches and the sense of discovery and wonder.  But as a new player today, the experience feels shallow.

I will break the game down into four buckets and go over each:  Base building, resource gathering/farming, vehicle play, discovery.

In each of those 4 major game segments, they managed to have some twist/quirk that makes it either annoying, tedious, unsatisfying, or pointless to do.  

[h1] Base Building: [/h1]
Not great.  You can build using wall/roof/floor tiles (think Fallout 4) or you can build using pre-fab rooms and tunnels (think SubNautica).  The Fallout 4 style is executed very poorly.  The tiles are all very "tiley", so your base ends up looking very blocky and "Minecraft"-ish, and just doesn't look like it belongs in that world visually.   Building using pre-fabs will give you a base that visually matches the rest of the gameworld more, but you're limited somewhat in the creativity due to those pre-fab shapes.   

And then there are things that make you scratch your head and go, "What were they thinking?"  

There's only one kind of bed.  Remote trade terminal can only be placed in pre-fab structures.  Certain lighting fixtures will only turn on if built in a pre-fab structure.  You have to string ugly wire through out the room to power many interior lamps and lights.  The camera angle while building is annoying and you have to utilize glitches to achieve camera angles that is better for base-building.  A lot of the common pre-fabs for underwater bases require Crystal Sulphide, an annoying resource to get, can only be sourced in the wild and underwater, and each resource node only yields 3 units of the Crystal Sulphide.

But even if you spend the time and build something epic, it still feels like an abandoned building at the end.  Because you can't get more than 5 NPCs into your base, and those NPC's are stationary.

[h1] Resource Gathering/Farming: [/h1]
Also not that great.  There's a bunch of resources in the game, but most of demand revolves around a dozen or so.  Gathering them isn't a fun activity.  Point at something, hold down mouse 1, wait until the something disappears, point at something else, repeat.  While that can be satisfying for a while, after the 30th planet you land on, it starts to feel pointless.  Wealth accumulation can happen very quickly even for new players, so you can just buy any resources you need instead of mining.  There are just too many less tedious and faster ways to gain resources.  

Trying to hunt for a cool multi-tool (a mining tool, weapon, and scanner all-in-one) can be rewarding, but also tedious due to the heavy RNG nature of this game.

[h1] Vehicle Play: [/h1]
The only part of the game that held some value IMO.  Finding a cool looking ship, decking it out, and cruising around in it is definitely fun.   Hunting/farming for a badass capital ship (basically your personal space station with a base) and frigates (a fleet you can send out to missions, think Assassin's Creed Black Flag) is also rewarding.  The ground vehicles can use a bit of rework to make them more worthwhile, but those are still fun to use overall.  

However, most of the activities you will do in a vehicle are not very challenging.  So having a junk ship can still get you through 99.9% of the game content just fine.  Unless you are trying to take out another capital ship, the vehicle combat is trivial.  You can't change the color of your spaceship, absolutely annoying.  You only get to have 6 ships at a time...in a game world with 13 trillion solar systems, each with their own 21 possible types of ships, you get to hold SIX.  Listen developers, how about you take away 3 trillion solar systems and let me keep two more ships?  I'll try to make the best out of the 10 trillion solar systems left, I promise.

[h1] Discovery: [/h1]
The biggest draw of this game, arguably.  Yet it's totally disappointing.  Yeah, there are near infinite systems and planets to discover, but you will start seeing the same things over and over pretty quickly.  The creatures still look ridiculous.  Just a bunch of earth lifeform body parts mixed and matched together in ridiculous proportions.  Occasionally, some lifeform will actually look "alien", like a floating cube, or a hopping mushroom thing.  

The planets aren't that special, and don't really have any surprises.  If you land on one spot on the planet and look around, you can safely expect the rest of the planet to look just like that.  And after a dozen star systems or so, you've pretty much seen everything there is to see.

When every planet/creature is special, no planet/creature is special.

The game presents all the content too quickly.  If you play the 5+ hours daily like I did, you will reach "endgame" in about a week.  I consider "endgame" as having finished the main story quests, maxed out all equipment/ship, and still have enough resources to switch to any ship or capital ship in the game.  And endgame "content" is pretty much, 1) sitting around in different stations waiting for a cool ship to show up so you can buy it, 2) hopping around systems and planets trying to score that really cool multi tool, 3) building some magnum opus base, or 4) running missions for Quicksilver currency to buy cosmetics.  

You can find alot of good ship and multi tool locations on discords and reddit, but taking away that hunt makes the game even less fulfilling. 

Ships spawn with randomized stats, but any ships can be upgraded to the highest class and inventory capacity, so good ship vs not-good ship is totally based on your personal opinion on how the ship looks.

But after your ship(s) is maxed out, the fun-factor drops.  Because there's nothing to do with all that power.  The vast majority of the content is completely unchallenging.  One-shotting enemies with 45k damage, doesn't feel all that different than one-shotting them with 15k damage.   Would you like to smash ants as Mike Tyson, or would you like to smash ants as The Hulk?  No difference.  Being able to become a centi-millionaire and able to buy pretty much any ship you want in the first week, doesn't feel fun.

Some other "discovery-related" annoyances:
You can't return to a place you've been unless you drop a beacon or write down the coordinates, planet name, and system name of the place.  Your screen ends up spammed with beacon icons or you just have to settle with possibly never returning to that spot again.  Even if you drop a beacon, you still have to remember the system and be in that system to see what beacons you have there.  

You can't open the galaxy map unless you're in a star ship AND in space.  Sometimes you just want to check the map and plan, without having to get into a ship, take off, fly to space just to do it.  Plus take off's expend resources, if you're not on a designated landing area or a space station, so you can literally be expending resources just to check the galaxy map. 

There are still bugs, but many of them benefit the player so you might not see too much complaint.  i.e. Duping bugs.  Being able to collect objective rewards without spending the resources.

[h1] Bottomline [/h1]

The game isn't fun.  It dumps 5 years worth of content on you immediately, and the feeling progression and accomplishment is gone after just a couple of days. My favorite YouTube video came out before the game was released; "No Man's Sky - The Horrible Truth" by Weebl, makes me laugh to this day. But my friend pleaded with me to get it, so the Steam Summer Sale brought it down to a price that I would feel only moderately abashed paying if it was as bad as I thought it was.

It has become a very addictive experience, held my interest, and I have really enjoyed: 1. discovering languages, 2. discovering planets, 3. hunting and digging for whatsits and gidgets.

The multiplayer connection, interaction, trading, and questing is fantastic. We found only a few glitches with doing missions together, but nothing breaking or too disappointing. Connecting with your friend was so smooth, and painless that we thought we were doing something wrong and had to keep checking if we were connected. Loading into a friend's game host and bringing your inventory, everything you have already experienced and built, rather than starting all over, is simply game industry revolutionary.

The only problem that I have had is that every other time that I load the game up in VR, the textures are scrambled and look something like a unicorn threw up after doing copious amounts of heavy narcotics.

I really don't understand what the haters are hating on.

I don't understand how people are saying this game is fixed. Granted, I only played for about an hour and played a few different single player worlds. But those worlds were near identical in how they were made: the creatures and plants only varied by color or shape, and all the resources look exactly the same despite the wildly different environments.

This game has so much potential, but they need to fix the random world generator. It's so immersion breaking going from a -58C frozen world, to a 20C toxic world and seeing almost identical creatures and plants. Something like the poisonous exploding plant pods is cool in the 20C toxic world, but doesn't really make sense in the -58C frozen world. The game also needs to modify the near same exact nondescript 4 legged dinosaur like creature to fit it's environment: A thick hide might be helpful in a 20C toxic world, but shouldn't they have fur or something to keep them warm at -58C (I mean polar bears can only survive to about -45C from a quick google search). 

The game also simply does not look like the pictures shown. Granted sometimes the random world generator does gets it right and makes a great looking world. However I don't think it's very fun restarting the game over and over until you get a cool looking world to play on. I also don't think it's great to say you just have to keep playing until you find a good looking planet. Each biome could easily be made better by giving them unique plants and animals, as well as different looking "things to click" for the resource nodes (because again, blue hydrogen crystals and yellow sodium flowers get old fast and don't make sense if they are all the same on every single world). 

There is also still the issue of creatures or even the player just clipping through objects. It does not seem like resources that you can collect or most of the trees will interact with the player or other creatures. So you're walking around and creatures are walking through trees and rocks. The weather and "storms" in the game are a complete joke. I got caught in a blizzard, and all it does is apply some debuffs and put on a frozen screen effect. Creatures just keep walking around, the sky didn't change or start snowing or anything. There also don't appear to be very many animations, so a lot of the game play was pointing the laser gun at some rocks, standing there holding E to collect something, or going through menus, and it honestly makes it feel like it's still in alpha.

[h1]Summary - TLDR[/h1]
Absoulutely visually and aurally stunning game. I heard how good it's got since its disastrous release and I did not expect it to be this good. It has lots of content and for 60 dollars, mod-free, it has more content than most other open world games I've played. 
[hr][/hr]
[h2]The piloting experience[/h2]
As an Elite Dangerous fan, this game's space experience may not be as aurally mind-blowing, visually impressive or challenging, but its simplicity is its strong point as well, allowing players to actually play and enjoy the rest of the game easily without needing items to bring mined objects back, or specific weapon mounts for specific jobs, or the challenge of docking with space stations and landing on planets manually. 

This helps especially when resource gathering is a key aspect to advancing in-game, helping players to easily and quickly do what's needed to be done, instead of grinding for hours just to auto-dock, automatically retrieve mined asteroids and more. 

[h2]Base building[/h2]
Compared to other building-centered games and games that did not focus on base building but added the feature later on, NMS has got an amazing building system that allows players to express their creativity really well. It for sure cannot beat something like the versatility of Parkitect's building system but it does the job better than I imagined. Sure we are missing features like putting items inside of items or lots of basic shapes for custom architecture, but it does a lot right as well.

It allows us to create the bases of our dreams with the basic structure blocks relatively inexpensively and also gives us the necessary tools to decorate the interiors quite well. The short walls allows us to add depth to the builds, which is a nice touch.

[h2]Power and Logic[/h2]
This game also strikes it well with its power system, its not as complex as something like Minecraft's Gregtech mod but its simplicity allows beginners to easily understand the way it works and use it. Items like the power inverter helps players to create logic gates and allows us to create all sorts of mechanisms such as automatic doors, player activated lights and proximity-based machine states (turning them on only when the player is near, saving power, for example)

After watching the train wreck that was the launch of this game, I am delighted to say that this game is worth every cent, sale or no sale. It was fun and engaging and I had a great time playing with my friend for hours at a time. The game can be so engrossing that often, the only thing that stopped us from playing was one of us being on clock duty and saying hey its time to call it a night. 

Pros: 
1. Exploration and freedom to do so. Once you get your ship and do a few missions this game opens up and leaves you to go at your pace. Want to go off and explore the galaxy and ignore the main quest... it lets you and actually rewards you for it. 
2. Quality of Life. This game is the rare game that almost every decision is made from the design perspective of "would this improve or hurt the fun of playing this game". There are few areas where the game "punishes" you just for punishment sake. For example bag space is rarely an issue. You are limited at first but there are multiple ways, easy and hard, cheap and expensive, to increase your bag size to the point that you have to TRY to fill it up. 
3. Updates on the regular. There seems to be an active update schedule that makes the game feel fresh and cared for. The developers seem to care about the product and it shows. 

Cons: 
1. This is a single player game first and foremost. The systems in place to allow multiplayer are there but they are added on. This game was not made for multiplayer from the ground up. I played with a friend in coop for my entire play through and 100% achievement run. Though it worked, to say that it was smooth would be a lie.

TLDR: If it's on sale and you like survival, crafting, exploring games, pick it up. At full price, depending on your budget, it's still a pretty good deal.

Enjoy the creativity to build a base... The nominal 'uses' for said base are limited, but real. If, however, you just want to build something cool they have you covered.

Explore parts of the galaxy that are procedurally generated including the plant and animal life. Yes, there is a lot of sameness to those generations, but often just as I would get bored with the same old chicken-raptor on the moon something bizarre or interesting would appear.

There's a story line that would be as equally compelling just reading than it is 'playing' through. I enjoyed it, but didn't feel like the game mechanics made it feel particularly epic. Essentially it was mostly travel (which often amounts of a lot of jumps - may as well be one long loading screen.) Still, kudos for some of the ideas presented and how they were exposed.

Collect a bunch of semi-random ships that basically follow a few basic shapes, plus a couple of weirder ones. The Living Ship addition was pretty interesting, for example. Not much to say here. Like the Exocraft, your suit and multitool, and even a Capitol Ship, there's a grindy MMO-like aspect to all of these things that *feels* like it's about to present you with micropayments. There might be a point of gamer pride in, say, finding an extremely rare combination of ship parts, if it wasn't for the fact that the game really does run on a local save file that the unscrupulous/lazy can simply edit to achieve whatever they wish. I don't blame the folks that do this, but it certinaly takes the shine off of many 'hard' achievements in the game when you know about it. 

As of this review (6.28.2021) I feel like I've pretty much finished the game as it is... But wait, there's likely to be more!

Though this game was panned as incomplete on release, the devs have certainly earned redemption. It's not perfect by any stretch. A lot of activities are unexciting, trivial or needlessly repetitive. But for every one of those, there's something fun or interesting or just weird. There's a lot of content for the game as it stands and I feel like I'm 'done' with it for now, but I certainly see myself returning to it in the near future as they add more content.

TLDR: Those looking for a good survival game may be rather bored. However, if you aren't concerned with that, and you are just in it for the exploration, crafting, and base building, then this game's got what you want.

I am mostly writing this to bump the score. This game's rating still suffers from its reception at release. While it may have deserved  a low score at the time, that is absolutely not reflective of its current state. 

If you like open world sandbox and exploration, don't hesitate to pick this one up. The team has been hard at work for YEARS pumping out fun and interesting content updates, turning No Man's Sky into the incredible experience that it was supposed to be. There is a LOT to do now, and Hello Games has not shown any sign of stopping. 

The one thing that I want to point out is that while this game is listed as being an "open world survival crafting game", the survival elements are INCREDIBLY light. If you are looking for a survival game, I would look elsewhere - the current survival elements exist mainly to create hostile environments in dangerous areas. There IS a survival mode, but it mostly just ups the difficulty and adds inventory loss upon death. This is fine, but it doesn't change the fact that the existing survival elements are still quite lightweight and surface level. That being said, Hello has released multiple overhaul updates already, so who knows what may come in the future.

Heard all this great stuff about how great NMS had become since launch.  Figured I'd fire it up.  Started a Normal game.  Spawned into a zone with some kind of high "toxicity" stuff on the planet, so I was dying in the first 15 minutes; in a desperate attempt to decipher the UI and save myself, died to falling damage.  20 minutes in.  Tried a new game.  Less "toxicity", more radiation.  Same deal.  Total time to second point 45 minutes.

The game's UI is one of the most user-unfriendly ones I've ever laid eyes on.  New players have no guidance on how to navigate the UI at all.  Basically, the entire "difficulty" of this game is just trying to decipher a shitty interface so you don't die, then scrambling to find the mats you need to not die, then maybe you get a few minutes to figure out the rest of it while sitting in some cockpit of your broken spaceship so you don't die to a toxic rainstorm or some such thing.

Definitely a sad experience compared to Valheim (which is still punishing in terms of death penalty but has a much, much, much more intuitive UI, while ramping up difficulty more gradually as you progress in terms of travel from your home base and/or unlocking additional horde attacks) or even 7 Days To Die (which has a much better UI overall, better control of difficulty and death penalty, and other features that make it easier to get into, even while being pretty punishing during blood moon hordes).  If your idea of fun is spending hours trying to figure out how to play a game, then NMS is definitely a good fit.  If you're looking for something you can just fire up and start playing and "get" pretty fast so you can dive into the game, I'd just wait for Starfield from Bethesda and see if it gets the same modding community love that FO4 and Skyrim got (my bet is, it will).

Reviews.106016:
This game saved my life.

I am 29

My ex-wife and I have a daughter together, and adopted our son together. They are now both 4 years old.

When we were going through our separation, I found myself lost and miserable. I was self destructive. I got so mad one day from everything spiraling out of my control that I punched some concrete in a moment of overwhelming emotion. That caused me to break my 5th metacarpal in my right hand... my working hand... my games hand.. the hand that I held and carried my children to bed with.. The hand I desperately needed to make sure I could continue to provide.

After learning of the severity of my self-inflicted damage, I was borderline su-c-dal. Keep in mind that just a few months before this, I was the happiest man with no history of depression or anxiety. I have never had fits of rage, or been one to break down and cry, but I was in a low spot that just really buried me from being able to see the light on the other side.

Having nothing better to do, I searched for a game I could play, ONE HANDED while I recovered. I somehow stumbled upon this game and read some of the reviews. I decided that it had to be worth a shot... I must admit, I didn't beat the game, or play nearly as long as some of you. In fact, I may have only played this game a day or two.. With that being said, after doing so, I had a new found joy and hope for life. I was able to put behind me the pain and suffering that had been cast over me. I was able to experience other peoples joy and happiness. I was able to see the fruits of my "labor". I relaxed for 5 ♥♥♥♥♥♥♥ minutes to this music long enough to realize that I was going to be okay.

After coming to that realization, I turned the game off, and I went back to work. It hurt my hand like hell but I was motivated. I stopped feeling so damn sorry for myself, and I became the father I needed to be in that moment, not the weak boy I was behaving as.

Today, I am close friend with my kids mother. We don't fight, or argue, or say hurtful things to each other. We are parents, and friends.

I now have 3 kids. My third child is, wait for it, ALSO 4 YEARS OLD. The woman I am with was going through a very similar situation at the time of my own separation, and we just stumbled in to each others life unexpectedly. We have been in a relationship for a year now, and are very happy together.

Moral of the story, you never know what life holds in store for you, and if I would have given up when all the odds were stacked against me, I wouldn't be where I am today. This silly little game helped me realize that.

Thank you

No Man's Sky is nothing like the title that it was when it first launched itself onto the PCs of thousands of excited gamers. What started as a mess of a game has over time become an intergalactic exploration game with near infinite replayability, through free update after free update. No Man's Sky offers nearly infinite planets to explore, each one filled with wildlife, flora, and minerals to discover. While this does get somewhat repetitive, there's tons more to do, from quests, to the story, to base building, to finding and buying new ships, to digging up artifacts, to learning different languages, there is always something to do. The customization options available to you when it comes to your ship upgrades, suit upgrades, tool upgrades, you're able to customize a lot. Base building allows for some great creativity and freedom in creating what you want. If you're looking for a survival exploration game with near infinite content, No Man's Sky is the game for you.

[h1]Definitely better than it used to be.[/h1]
Out of principle I'd only grab this on a 50%+ sale, mostly because the idea of charging full price on a nearly 5 year-old title is a bit silly.
Then again, No Man's Sky is a bit silly. A game repeatedly bashed and/or praised over the years for its ridiculously rocky development cycle, and initial broken promises/dreams.

But I can't deny that I'm actually having fun with it now. Multiplayer in particular brought a lot of life into the game, with lobbies (the Nexus) and pretty smooth intercontinental connection helping to provide a much more solid, rounded experience.

That isn't to say the game's perfect, heck no. You're still likely to encounter a fair few bugs on any given playthrough, [b]but[/b] the gamebreaking ones have mostly been squashed. You'll occasionally hear about 'em, but in my 134 hours the worst I've encountered has been slingshotting (extreme rubberbanding when the DNS goes trippy).

[b]So, what's changed?[/b]
The last time I [i]really[/i] tried NMS was 2019, when it was still pretty shaky in terms of resource balancing and exploration. It was excessively frustrating to keep having to spend several minutes farming carbon/ferrite for basic components/fuel because you just needed so MUCH of it all the time.

Now? I can't say for sure what the exact number balancing was, but it's far less tedious. You can easily grab what you need and keep moving on - and pretty early on you'll learn that time is more valueable than money, buying all the ferrite, carbon, and oxygen at the first space station as you can buy to save yourself time hunting those resources on-world.

It leaves you more time to actually explore the world, rather than stare at rocks as you mine them down.

[b]Brief Pros:[/b]
[list]
[*]Planet variety is pretty decent, with biome/resource/danger levels and changes to boot
[*]Character customization is good, with some unlockable parts from daily quests in the Nexus available
[*]Planets feel more alive, thanks to PRISMS changing animal densities
[*]The Nexus allows for temporary party formation on quests, so you're not stuck with a random after the quest is done
[*]Companions are a fantastic addition, allowing you to hatch eggs and genetically alter the outcomes (colours, mutations, size and behaviour)
[/list]

[b]Brief Cons:[/b]
[list]
[*]Variety overlap does happen the further you get into the game, and very frequently at that
[*]Exocrafts (vehicles) are still pretty "meh" in terms of usefulness; you and your ship can clear the game just fine
[*]Companions are limited to 6 slots - far too few for how many unique species there are (set or random)
[*]The gameplay loop does dry out, but it doesn't happen 'til a long ways in for most now (I'd say 100+ hours without burnout is pretty darned good for any game, honestly)
[/list]

As for the story? Well.. it's [i]interesting[/i], but has a problem with trying to beat you over the head with the Do-You-Get-The-Reference-Yet Bat, if you're at all familiar with the concept of Science Fiction. The topics it touches on are pretty fascinating, but depending on your viewpoint they can either be things to ponder on, or things to wonder what the point of bringing it up even was.

I say it's definitely worth a try today. It's much friendlier in terms of time investment and resource grinding.

Reviews.106168:
I am this |   | close to recommending it, but the game fails at several basic points that makes me unable to recommend it even several years after its release.



Let's talk player housing:

Completely unnecessary, not fully thought out and boring. Yes some people can build fancy bases and I guess it's better to have base building than not since it could be optional. However think about other games in which you have player housing and why. In MMOs? Crafting. In Minecraft? Storage and crafting.

Why do we even have player housing in NMS? What does it do? What is it for? Oh right, artificial quests. You gotta build this and that to progress a quest so you can unlock the recipes you need in order to play the game and do what you want.

Why do I think this is a problem? Because it changes the pace of the game and makes it worse. We already have spaceships. We have huge inventories in both our backpack AND ships. Why would we need a base? Why can't we just craft stuff inside our ship? We can craft materials in our ship or on foot anyway, so why can't we just have ship interiors? This would make way more sense than having bases. Maybe if we needed to store our items somewhere a base would be useful, but it's just not. Anything a base COULD do in NMS the ships could do better.

Another problem is that it's not even worth keeping materials around. It's better to just sell everything for money and buy back what you need from a station. Or if you need something basic you just gather it from the surroundings. We could have storage like in superior games like Minecraft and Satisfactory, but we don't.



Next on the agenda is factory/production:

This is a disgrace. No matter how you do it, you are doing it wrong. This is because either you rush to the end and have no progression which feels empty and sucky, OR you do it in order and have some progression but then you're wasting your time and feel awful for wasting time.

In a proper game like Factorio or Satisfactory you may start out needing cement to build something. You use that to get iron which you build more stuff with. Later you get coal to upgrade the iron to steel and so on. eventually you get to exotic materials and stuff and it feels great because you went through meaningful progression. Here in NMS you just skip to the end with 0 progression or you are wasting time.

NMS is made in this weird way where you need a crappy engine to jump to a star system farther away, then you need a normal engine to jump to systems farther away than that, and then you get a good engine to jump to the farthest places. The problem? There's no freaking point! What everyone does is they build an engine, jump, buy the materials, build the next engine, jump, buy the materials, build the next engine, jump, start their industry and have over 100 million income per day forever.



That brings us to the crap economy of NMS:

On your FIRST DAY you can setup passive income that gives you over 100 million a day. Keep in mind that the most expensive thing in the game is gonna be around 150 million. This makes it feel like you've already beaten the game since you can afford every ship, weapon, freighter and upgrade with ease. Of course if you do not set this up then you'll feel like you are wasting time.

Another issue is the borked economy. If you sell items to a vendor the items will now be worth less than before since the vendor has more of it. You simply sell to a vendor, buy it all back and you now have your original items AND a profit. People sometimes abuse this by jumping around to different vendors to take all their cash and resources.



The MAIN gameplay:

Obviously the main thing NMS is made for is exploration. Why is this bad? Because everything looks the same. You have slight variations of biomes and species, but ultimately everything looks incredibly similar. This is supposedly what a huge amount of the playerbase bought the game for though, and they seem to like seeing the same flying rhino with slightly different toes dozens of times.



In conclusion:

NMS needs even more polish. It needs a better way to buy ships, better factory stuff, a better economy and pretty much several complete overhauls.

No Man's Sky starts you off in a hazardous world where you have to scavenge the nearby materials to survive. Eventually, you gather enough to fix your suit and your spaceship. From there, it becomes a game of base-building, trading, and interstellar exploration. There are story and side missions to complete, trying to solve a galaxy-wide mystery. The game does an excellent job of pacing, you're always learning something new without it being overwhelming.

There's definitely a few little things that could be dealt with better -- some UI icons are never properly explained and you may end up Googling a thing or two. Some random space encounters seem like they're there to just "be cool", so you'll spend a while flying around a mind-reading cosmic entity or an old destroyed space station only to find that they don't contribute to your progress at all. Maybe you'll get some cash or a couple of resources, but miss the prompt telling you that because there's suddenly 5 UI elements competing to get your attention.

Usually though, the UI is fine (once you understand it) and the interesting or useful random encounters outweigh the negatives.

VR is fantastic with this game. And with the most recent visual update, it looks incredible. My one and only issue is that the terrain manipulator's size can be adjusted very easily with mouse+keyboard, but the VR controls are counter-intuitive. For the most part the VR controls are great, but for this one particular issue it would make sense if we had wrist controls for adjusting the size rather than grip controls when having the other hand's wrist menu open. That sentence makes more sense when you've played in VR.

This game definitely has some flaws, but honestly I'm enjoying my time with it. I can give it a solid recommendation.

When this game first came out, I heard that the reviews were terrible, largely due to the lack of any content. Let me just say that having only purchased the game since after the first few updates, I cannot even imagine this as a game without those updates. The updates were massive, totally "game changing" (pun intended), and because I only purchased the game after that, I have no experience of this game being anything other than wonderful and engaging.

Even since then, there have been multiple, massive, content additions and there is just so much to do. I love exploring, building, and building a bit of an economy. I always love economics and finances in games, and there's enough of that in this game to keep me interested, along with all the other content.

The graphics are a bit more cartoony than I'm used to, and I do have a friend that was turned off by that, but I found myself enjoying the game even though that's not usually my favourite visual style.

I will say that the first hour or so of the game can be extremely frustrating, and I felt that things just weren't clear enough for me to be happy with the tutorial. Maybe I'm just dense, but it was quite a frustration to not be certain how to do some things without googling. Most notably, I can only play this game in first person because the third person seems to have the camera not only behind but also a bit to the side, and I simply cannot deal with the controls intuitively from that angle. That said, I love playing in first person mode, so that's not a problem at all.

There are several story lines, and they all seem fairly mysterious and also dark. They're not overwhelmingly dark, but dark enough that it's not particularly to my own taste. That said, you're not really forced to get into the story, and you can totally just ignore the dialogue and follow the mission instructions. After you get through the tutorial, instructions are much clearer, and I totally forget the frustration I had at the beginning.

Overall, I'd say that my experience isn't perfect, and I do have a few frustrations, but I do absolutely adore this game in the end, and I'm about to fire it up again as soon as I finish this review. I think 303 hours is a decent sign that I do enjoy it.

This review is more about certain specific details, and not really a full review. I'm sure there are plenty more general takes, but I wanted to add a few thoughts on smaller points whilst also putting a "positive" review on the pile.

It's a lot of tweaking and praying to get VR running smoothly, even on a RTX 3090. But this is basically Crysis for VR. It's the best VR game I've ever played and I absolutely love just floating in my space ship or watching the starry night sky.  On top of all that, the game itself has come so far from it's humble (and uh...scandalous) beginnings. It's really amazing how much effort and work they've put into it. There's not a lot of plot but the Alone Amongst the Stars story line really hits hard.  I've been here off and on since the very beginning, when those of us that liked the game were hiding in /r/nomanshigh.

I'm not here to legislate the game's launch, we've all settled into our views on that one way or another.  But I will say that even for someone who enjoyed the base game for a while, the game today is absolutely nothing like that and has really grown into it's own.  It's still a bit grindy but the grind is self directed. Do you wanna explore? Build your base a bit? Work up some money for a new freighter/ship/multitool? It's all up to you and there's several ways to do it all.

(Also Derelict Freighters are super cool and creepy as heck in VR.  Doooooo eeeeet.)

That said, I wouldn't recommend buying this strictly for VR unless you already have everything and are willing to tune it for a few days to get comfortable.  However, I spun it up in pancake mode the other day and had no idea what the controls were, for a gauge of how long and how often (a long time, all the time) I play in VR over Oculus Link to my Quest 2.

-100% cross-platform drop-in/out co-op

-VR Support

-Hours worth of gameplay

"Shigeru Miyamoto: A rushed game is forever bad"

Law of physics is an undeniable fact, until proven wrong. All scientific data, theories and rules are there simply because they could not be proven wrong. But what I've always been taught, we learn facts, that that we accept as rules, theories and laws because they couldn't be proven wrong with our technology or understanding at the time. One of my professors always said to keep an open mind and treat everything as a theory, where behind each law lies a secret remaining to be discovered and change our perspective. He taught me that everything in the universe in a way, has an exception from its normal occurrence. No Man's Sky is one of these exceptions.

Hello Games had some trouble before the release and a ton of the game was supposedly lost due to a flood. While Sean Murray did speak things that were not true upon the release, it took them years to fix the game and I am very happy to be an somewhat early buyer of NMS. I've participated in the process of updating the game from early, undeniably bad stages, up to what game it is right now.

And right now this is the best space exploration game there is available. It's casual, but extremely beautiful, it's set on exploration of unique (randomly generated) worlds and searching for upgrades for your weapons, suits or ships. There is story in the game, however I just lose myself in exploring worlds, over and over. Now the game runs pretty well and there are no issues that I've found so far. Moreover the game supports mods - which can do pretty much anything such as making you walk faster, change parameters of jetpacks etc. So you can just change your game to whatever you'd like it to be - even add spaceships!

Trying to explain the gameplay would seem boring in words and even in gameplay, but the thrill you get from entering the atmosphere of a new world or to pursue the next thing is not easy to convey. If you're a fan of casual space exploration and progress, like to see vistas or explore caves - this game is for you!

It may have taken a couple of years, but this game is finally something closer to what we all thought we were getting when we pre-ordered.  When this game was released, it basically boiled down to:  Mining resources so that you could fly to another planet and mine the same resources, so you could eventually warp to another system and do the same thing.  It was repetetive after an hour and the game equivalent of a migraine headache about 10 hours in.

Here's what changed:

-More missions and story.... like LOTS!!!
-More varied resources, plants and animals.
-Base building with teleporters so you can return to particularly good planets by building a base there.
-NPCs in your base who give you missions and help you get better equipment.  They're a bit like a slow in game tutorial.
-MULTIPLAYER!!!  While the game is still true to it's word that you don't really ever run into other players as the universe is too big, it's not possible to invite friends to your base, join other's games or summon an anomoly that lets you play missions with others.
-Fleet battles and a friegher where you can park all of the ships you've found and claimed.  I still need to explore this feature more as I keep spending all my units on exosuit upgrades.

What could still be better:
-Mapping.... Galaxy and system mapping is still clunky as shit, and there is still no such thing as a planet map.
-Space combat... considering how many pirates try to steal your loot they could have at least added support for joysticks and controllers here.  Currently, the combat is more of a nuisance than a feature.

My final thoughts:
This game is FINALLY worth the money we paid at pre-order, but space combat still needs a LOT of work.

No Man's Sky is good for vibing. It's the kind of game where you worry less about working towards a goal and think more "I'll get there eventually by screwing around." It's got a good mix of relaxing and exciting gameplay.

The gameplay mechanics, while not anything revolutionary in their own right, work well to encourage this playstyle. You get currency just by cataloging the procedural plants and animals, for example. Most resources have broad applications, so even if you're just collecting stuff with no purpose for it yet it'll almost certainly be useful down the line. You rarely have to stress over something specific. And if you want the game to give you a specific goal to work toward, you can use mission boards at space stations to get tasks.

The procedural planets are a mix of planets that look kind of the same and absolutely wild unique worlds. You'll find a system with the tenth green mushroom planet of the day, and also a planet that's an endless meadow of golden grass and purple trees. The generation could definitely use work to make individual props look more unique (every single planet has the same flytrap plant for example) but the planets overall can look very unique, and they're almost always incredibly pretty looking. I have over 50 screenshots.

Exploring the planets is made fun by the variety of ways to move around. You can fly over the surface with your spaceship, use one of the land vehicles, or tame and ride the procedural animals. Or just walk, which the jetpack makes entertaining on its own.
Some planets are fairly tame, while others have massive storms or are covered in angry robots. The more extreme worlds have valuable resources to encourage you to explore the surface and get mad cash. This is the exciting part of the game I mentioned. The game uses valuable items to encourage players to stick around on dangerous worlds, and evading sentinels or hiding from storms while filling your inventory with garbage worth millions of units is a lot of fun.

Exploring the galaxy is far from the only thing you can do. You can build bases, make farms, or follow longer quests for example. The amount of stuff to do in the game is impressive, but it never feels overwhelming since there's never a rush to do any particular thing. You can take your time and focus on whatever catches your interest the most.

Good game for people who want to stop and scan the space roses.

The game was alright but not worth the money they are asking. 
I bought this game in early 2021 with my girlfriend and played with her and built our house.

A houses are pretty basic and glitchy + laggy.
Don't think of trying to build underground unless you want your bases to be constantly looking like a garbage heap. 
If you like flying from place to place then this is kinda fun. The space combat the alright, the ground combat is boring and .... yeah lets say it again, real boring.

The graphics are beautiful and the procedurally generated planets are beautiful however after the first 3-4 galaxies worth of planets the monsters, plants and fauna just start to become much of a much-ness without any real great difference.
The own a pet is .. pointless and looks kinda okay but again nothing to write home about.
The space ship differentiation is interesting however the fact that you can't repaint or alter the look of the ships in any way is a real turn down and something which is such a basic function one must think it's intentionally done to "grind" to get that perfect looking and statted space ship.

The greatest thing for the game though I must say is the developers. I'm aware they were total a-holes with their promises pre release and were treated as snake oil salesmen however they have been constantly working hard on this game pumping out patch after patch quality of life changes. I think one day this game WILL be real great and fun to play. Just not today at this point in time, theres just not enough to keep me interested and stay.


The quests are... total garbage glitch.
The interraction between power and batteries and wiring is also pretty bad and needs work.
The chat interface is poor to say the least.

So overall 

Combat 5/10 (8/10 for starship 2/10 for land)
Crafting systems 6/10
Graphics 9/10
Scope 10/10
Gameplay 4/10
Replayability 2/10
Storyline 2/10
Endgame ?/10 (there isn't really any serious start so there can't really be an end can there).
Sound 5/10
In game voices 1/10 garbage

Overall, I would say this game is great. It has interesting exploration and can be quite relaxing, especially when playing with friends. Cross platform play is supported, so if you have friends on other devices you can play with them. Super addictive so don't play at night if you have work the next day.

The downsides are present however. The game can oftentimes feel grindy for things such as nanites and rare materials, however, it isn't on the levels of a MMO or Graveyard Keeper. The bugs are everywhere, not just in the sense of the game creatures, but the programming. In one night of playing for about three hours I encountered about five different bugs such as: not being able to talk to a captain of a frigate after helping fight off pirates, falling into the floor of said frigate and having to reload my save, a unlimited language learning glitch occurred that allowed me to learn fifty words before I stopped it, a friend getting completely stuck in a tree and having to reload, duplicating ships on accident so that a friend and I had the same salvaged ship. The list could go on into the often times accidental duplication glitch to glitchy meshes, but I digress. The game is still very entertaining and oftentimes relaxing even on survival mode. But do be aware that you will run into a few of the bugs

Reviews.106860:
An incredible game, truly like no other.  Depending who you are, that could be its best quality or its worst.

An endless, slow paced, peaceful journey through magnificent environments is exactly my thing. I love that there is no direction other than the one you seek out.  You can spend hours just cataloguing plants and animals, gathering wealth, or racking up light years across the galaxy.  You can embark on a mysterious quest to reveal the nature of the universe, and if you get tired mid way you can take a break and build something cool. No Man's Sky can be a sandbox or an extreme survival challenge; a multiplayer community or total isolation.  You can get into fights or complete missions - but you don't [i]have[/i] to do [i]anything[/i]. You can literally just enjoy wasting time. I know I do.

But I love games that let me just do my thing, without any direction or agenda.  I like to be allowed to [i]experience[/i] a game.  If you demand that a game must [i]entertain[/i] you, I'd suggest you leave this one be. It probably isn't your thing.

Reviews.106957:
TL;DR
It wasn't worth it at first, ...
but as an investment into a huge, space, sandbox, open universe, mmo game -- it's worth it in 2021. There's still a lot more big content patches being added to the game, to add. The game now has tameable animals, freighter ships, a multiplayer hub, vehicles, teleporters, a good character creator you access at every space station (free c-change respecs, you get presets for characters you'd like to switch to anytime) and more things I haven't noticed yet. This satisfies a minecraft niche, an elite dangerous niche with basic dumbed-down space travel, and spore now when you find new animals. The game still has abominations that makes no sense, but some animals make you want to tame them. I haven't found how to tame high-flying birds yet, but that WILL be a great patch when you can tame a dragon/ bird/ flying fish -- whatever you find in the sky. lol

The game has trouble loading some bases or when you enter to space sometimes. I have a gtx 1060, i7-8700 3.2ghz, 16gb ram -- all because there are no loading screens. It's seemless. When I upgrade to a better processor (my bottleneck), I may have no lag when loading all base-assets when entering a new region. Loading into the game after a while may be very long also (4+ minutes). So, take note. Have a decent amount of ram, and a good processor and gfx card if you want to run the game.

Grinding will feel slow, but if you find a nice place to start your first base, you'll enjoy the journey. I love the game now. NMS feels like a good AAA game, done right and its still growing with new features. NMS can replace multiple games at this rate and its amazing to watch with each new patch.

Reviews.107012:
Here are my thoughts so far without having completed the main quests yet.

Excellent Game.

Great sense of exploration, lovely atmosphere and incredible sense of immersion. Easy to get lost in. I'd recommend considering survival mode if you prefer a bit of a challenge, it limits the amount of resources you can carry which makes upgrades to storage a significant incentive which increases the sense of progression. The ship flying feels great, you can fly straight to a planet you see in the sky from one planet and land on it without a single loading screen. The graphics and music similarly don't disappoint occasionally leaving me in awe of my surroundings. 

A few negatives include that often planets are drab and boring due to the random generation, it can be totally hit or miss, more often than not the planet is pretty dull, but there are outliers to this rule with some very pretty planets. There are occasional bugs as well, nothing major but I would recommend saving relatively frequently on the off chance something does go wrong, though autosave does update frequently enough to prevent any major time loss. Additional flaws is that I could potentially see it becoming aimless at some point, however since I mostly play on permadeath, the desire to prepare myself for the story missions is enough of a direction for me to focus on, I just don't know what the post game incentive will be and I shall update my review once I reach it.

Definitely worth a buy, it's not popular now just because its a meme to like it, it's a genuinely great game if you like survival games. This one features an above average level of polish for the genre to boot.

This game is just bad. I heard and read alot of the older content when the game released and then waited even longer to play this game. From the feel of it, nothing has changed. Astroneer did a better job at making you feel like you are the only person on the planet and being alone as you survive. The sense of being alone in No Man's Sky quickly get dashed as some ship flies overhead 10 minutes into the game. These type of games, where exploration and survival is the main theme, have to walk a very tightrope. Valheim and Astroneer do this beautifully. I can spend time dorking around my base making things and producing a list of things that I need to find to push my adventure a little more over the horizon. No Man's Sky from the get go is pushing to other planets even before I have had the chance to really explore the planet I started on. 

The pacing of Astroneer and Valheim feels right. You make technologies and advance at a good pace. While there is no real story to be had in either game, No Man's Sky pushes it's story at you so fast that it overlaps itself. It feels disjointed and confusing. I am talking to the person that basically gets you into space AFTER I have already talked to those same people in space. I even ties back to being alone. I was finding people and talking to them but all the dialog from the stranger feels like you should have not meet those people yet.

If you really want to play this game, I would suggest watching some youtube videos before you do. This game teaches you nothing. There are some quests that you will get that kinda teach you how some of the items work but if you neven pick up that item, then you never get the quest. Forget about mods too. There is NOTHING that tells you how they work. It was only be accident that I figured out why my +10 to thrusters was not +10 thrusting. The simple act of putting mods with like technology is never explained.

At this point I am just tired and frustrated with all that I think is wrong with this game. Needing to leave the ground. Having technology and your inventory using the same space. Having to stop exploring because of the arbitrary need to farm mats to feed to some advanced future machine. Spending more time farming the mats so I can explore only to use those mats for mining and never getting to really explore. Do not even get me started on the whole party nonsense. I had to quit the game to leave and accidental party I joined BECAUSE I DO NOT KNOW HOW TO LEAVE THE PARTY BECAUSE THEY DO NOT TEACH YOU! Sorry to all people that I randomly invited. Why the made the interact key and the invite to party key the same, I will never know. Just add it the list of bad things in this game.

13 Hours in 

If you like grindy gameplay (I.E. Mining and Exploring) then this game is for you. Yeah, you're grinding a bit but the exploration of planets, caves, asteroids, space stations and many more  make the experience very enjoyable. Plus, you're never stuck with nothing to do. Plenty to get going with. Mining cobalt in order to sell for credits? Spend some time in some caves. Deciding to top up your oxygen and hazard protection? You're going to need a suitable base camp to start scouting from. And you're going to have to build that base yourself from scratch.

Plus there is space stuff. Bounties on pirates to collect (Space battles! Pew-Pew-Pew!) and asteroids to mine. Recently my galaxy map told me that a black hole had been spotted nearby and I have no idea what that entails yet, but I'm itching to find out.

So yeah, No Man's Sky is pretty damn fun right now.

Do you like wandering for hours in a beautiful, stupefyingly vast expanse with no real place to go? Do you like the feeling of being completely out of your depth and slowly learning? Do you actively ignore quest markers in open-world RPGs? If yes, you will enjoy the basics of this game. 

I can't comment on plot or story structure or quests/missions. I've done maybe 3 or 4. I've spent the entirety of my time at this review in 2 star systems and visited a total of 8 planets. What that means is, take this review with more than a grain of salt if you came to this game for an engaging story, cool npcs, or diverse game-modes. At this point I've only done solo exploring.

With that being said, I truly love this game. You will definitely get a lot of bang for your buck.
The only thing you really have to do in this game is get resources, and even in that aspect you get some options, which is nice. You can mine them and use them to make other resources.

No Man's Sky is a game that has managed to overcome its controversial past and become a decent experience, albeit requiring a specific mindset to be enjoyable. 

Specifically, the myriad of features of this game spread across the apocryphal infinite universe will get old very quick; seeing everything over and over again, examining the nonexistent minutiae in each world's variety. Despite these massive shortcomings, I still think it is a good game and it is one that I enjoy a lot. That is where the part about a 'specific mindset' comes in.

When playing this I always focus on a specific handful of systems where I name every planet and imagine their stories and histories. Doing so makes each system and its planets and features so much more meaningful, deep, and impactful. It produces a sort of oneness with the virtual universe of No Man's Sky. Thus, the 'mindset' required is, ironically, restraining oneself to a few systems and filling in the gaps the game leaves glaringly open.

No Man's Sky is an empty sandbox that leaves its filling up to the player. Those expecting a thorough experience out of the box with deep meaning should avoid this game. Those who are imaginative and enjoy the small things, filling the box, will very much enjoy this game.

Reviews.107311:
Despite the majority of reviews telling you otherwise, No Man's Sky hasn't actually changed since it's release. It is still a massive, empty void with no point to any of it's gameplay mechanics. 

Here's what we were promised: a universe full of possibilities where you can find a planet or creature that's genuinely so unique and special that no one else could ever see it. Instead of taking all the money they made to expand upon that idea, they chose to make scanning planets/creatures/tiny little rocks a meaningless little side chore you do for credits instead of the actual meat of the game. The one thing you came here for isn't actually here. There is no unique thing you can find. The most you get is copy pasted ancient ruins or alien buildings with nothing in them but aliens you can't form any sort of bond with. 

So what they chose to focus all their money and time on since release is a very uninspired attempt at storytelling, Ubisoft-esque questing mechanics (just checking off a list of boring missions making you waste time traveling point to point) and pointless base building. All of which were somehow enough to trick the general audience into believing they turned this into good game with actual content. In reality, it's just Ubisoft meets space Minecraft minus the vast possibilities of creativity, a decent crafting system, and a genuinely intense survival system (You cannot die in this game unless it's on purpose. Seriously. I've tested it. If you stand still, enemies will literally just miss you forever.). 

Anyways, don't believe the hype. It's still a bad game. It's endlessly vapid and completely soulless. Do not waste your money unless you just want a game to fly around pretty environments in, and if you want that, I highly suggest buying Outer Wilds instead. That's a space game with an actual beating heart featuring truly unique planets and an actually rewarding story.

Reviews.107370:
I found NMS to be a rather shallow experience. I was expecting something along the lines of Subnautica (plot-driven survival) but instead found it more akin to Minecraft (sandbox with little to no plot) but with less emphasis on crafting. It doesn't necessarily mean one can't have some fun in it, just that it wasn't for me.
Some thoughts:
- The game has a great sense of freedom, which is probably its strongest aspect. Many styles of play are accommodated. It lends itself well to speed- and challenge-running.
- The procedural generation means that there is a lot to [i]see[/i], but not really much to [i]discover[/i]. SPOILER: [spoiler]The game itself alludes to the lack of depth in the main quest, in its revelation that everything is merely a simulation.[/spoiler]
- There's a distinct lack of challenge in the game, even on Survival and PermaDeath difficulties where the developers have attempted to "gamify" the experience by adjusting the survival mechanics and item costs.
- I feel the game is overpriced compared to other games at its price point. Even with a 50% discount the current price for me is £20 GBP; there are many superior games I would recommend over this for that money or less.

I completed two playthroughs: a "full" playthrough on Normal difficulty and a PermaDeath challenge run where I bought nothing except Wiring Looms, a couple of Microprocessors for the main quest at the beginning and the HyperDrive travel upgrades.

An excellent space exploration game that really pushes the boundaries of what's possible. As long as you come to peace with the infinitely wide yet inch-deep core gameplay loop that plagues this genre, you'll have a good time as there are a lot of things to do and a lot of interesting planets and places to explore. Companions was such a huge update as well especially for solo players as the companions really breath life into your adventures and makes solo play a lot less lonelier than it used to be.

People have said enough about the good graces of Hello Games and we all have heard the word "redemption" with any conversation about No Man's Sky, and for good reason. I'll dispense with the gushing about the development of this game, but it's been good and will only get much, much better in time. Looking forward to how the journey continues.

disclaimer: I've been playing on and off since 2019, but am currently in the middle of a playthrough. I haven't completed the main story and do not intend to do so at the moment.

This game is a beast. In spite of it's chequered history, it has grown into a fantastic gaming experience.

Each update has been interesting in some major way, and added extremely helpful creature comforts that have made the game significantly more fun (and to me, it was already extremely interesting from 1.0) and it's *pretty*. The bulk of my playtime came shortly after the Atlas Rises campaign released, but I came back to the game when Prisms dropped and have spent about 20 hours with it in the past week and oh my goodness, what a splendid game this has become. I quite enjoyed my time with the game back in 2018, but the insane amount of new content that Hello Games has put out since Atlas makes No Man's Sky feel almost like a full on remake.

The Atlas Rises campaign still seems to be the main narrative driver, which is perfectly fine as it's a wonderful old fashioned space-faring mystery about unlocking the secrets of the galaxy, but the addition of multiplayer, especially The Nexus (the central online player hub/space station) really opens up the galaxy and makes it feel alive. There was something beautiful about the isolation of previous versions, the idea of being on your own as you navigated this massive universe, but the ability to team up or go solo whenever you want brings with it a freedom that far outweighs the few drawbacks it comes with.

The graphical and performance upgrades that Prisms introduce are not to be overlooked, either. No Man's Sky has always been pretty poorly optimized, and Hello Games was never very forthright about exactly what kind of rig you needed to run it on highest settings at a smooth frame rate (only ever listing the bare minimum requirements that are laughably misleading, with no recommended requirements), but Prisms brings with it a slew of graphical optimization that makes the game run much more smoothly while also looking markedly better. The option for Nvidia users to turn on DLSS is huge, as that black magic techno-sorcery does what it always does and somehow makes games look better while running smoother.

If you're looking for an epic survival-focused journey through the stars, there are few games now that can rival No Man's Sky in terms of gameplay or presentation.

Having played this game originally when it first released on Playstation, and again on PC through Steam, I can confidently say that I cannot in good conscience recommend this game. Let's look at the good and the bad.

The Good: The game is a solid exploration/crafting title in the mode of a Subnautica-type game, though with less strenuous survival aspects. The music is moderately enjoyable, and the overall gameplay loop is addictive, if you're into that sort of thing. Hello Games clearly cares a lot about this title, as they've worked on it consistently since its initial disastrous launch, and new features and updates are getting added all the time.

The Meh: Hello Games has always made a point of showing off the fantastic worlds the game can procedurally generate for you. What is not clear immediately, though, is that a lot of these worlds will all kind of look the same. Most worlds you will visit are flat, barren, inhospitable hellscapes populated by flora and fauna that all kind of look the same as the last planet you visited. Every world I visited was the exact same everywhere I looked. If a planet is mountainous with red lakes and mushrooms for plants, it will be like that across its entire surface. There are no discernable biomes, and often no features or landmarks to help you navigate without the assistance of your HUD.

The Actually Bad: The game just doesn't run very well. It's a pretty unstable game that doesn't seem optimized very well. I'm running a computer that's less than a year old with current, up-to-date hardware in it (I was fortunate to build my PC before the computer chip shortage made that impossible for a lot of folks). And yet, I cannot seem to run NMS for any length of time without experiencing crashes to desktop. This happens when loading the game, when in menus, when exploring the world, when rotating the camera -- in short, all the time. And there doesn't seem to be any rhyme or reason to it. And even when it's not crashing, it just doesn't run very well. There's stuttering, textures that refuse to load, weird pop-in issues and more.

Summary: I really wanted to like this game, which is why I endured several repeated crashes and hours of lost progress on more than one occasion. But I just can't recommend that anyone pick up this game.

The game went a long way, it made a significant turnaround and for that alone I can recommend it.
It became somewhat grindy, but in a way that it is 5-minutes-grindy. I mean you have multiple upgrade avenues which you can achieve in a very quick time. It's built around with casuals in mind, achieving small steps one at a time.
Worlds still have only one biome and can become stale, but there's at least a lot of diversity in the kinds of world.

Here's a technical downside, though.
Because the game was primarily developed and optimized for PlayStation 4 (which has 8 cores), it needs 8 threads or 8 cores to function properly. The system requirement of a Core i3 is nonsense. I know of no Core i3 or similar low-spec AMD CPU that has 8 threads available. If you don't have 4 cores AND hyperthreading or 8 cores without hyperthreading, the game won't work properly for you and you'll observe constant stutter because the game is periodically waiting on region regeneration which ought to be done in the background but could not because the Windows scheduler ran out of threads for realtime processing.
As such, the recommendation is tentative under the condition that you have 8 threads.
