I have already played this game for well over 140+hrs on my ps4, this was before visions was released however.

I am in a strange place where I crave to play this again, but with the hours already invested; I felt it would be better for the experience, to wait for the devs to slow down with adding new content. It's been two years now! Beginning to rethink my strategy here.

The additional content is added for free. Yes, that's free... What game developer does this nowadays? These guys do. These aren't minor additions either, the developers really are working hard to bring a lot of quality of life fixes and additions along with the periodic new content. The more the better I say, please keep them coming.

The game has come a very very long way since it's haphazard and frankly slightly embarrassing initial release. 

What was once sparse and unfulfilling, is now the complete opposite; immersive, engaging and rewarding. You can choose how in-depth you want to go, but really.. this isn't elite dangerous or star citizen. It is easy to pick up. Before you know it you will be scheming ways with how to afford that new star ship.

Today, just testing the game play alone is super immersive. It is easy to get lost among the countless planets in this seemingly endless universe.

The graphics are absolutely beautiful. If you have the system to play it at maximum settings, you will find that there are not many other games with which you can compare this. It is simply mind-blowing sometimes when little details catch your eye and momentarily distract you from the task at hand. 

An almost stargate kind of lore crossed with a story which could be best described as something from black mirror... To really oversimplify it. The truth, when revealed; is quite unique in a way. No spoilers here.

The game is great when played with friends but it really isn't necessary. Lone wolf is the bread and butter of this game, which can obviously be challenging, sometimes perplexing but still loads of fun.

Honestly it can be a bit of a grind in the later game, if you do not use all the tech at your disposal. Completionists beware: This is a big one.

Well worth the price at 50% off.

While I have been enjoying No Man's Sky every update, I find that I get bored extremely quickly once I realize how little there is to do on the planets you explore. Each update I find myself getting excited to try out the new features and give it a go but end up losing steam extremely quickly as soon as I land on a planet. Sure there is vast oceans of content to explore in this game, but it's all shallow. 

The general gameplay loop is travel to a new galaxy, land on some planets, scan and then leave once you realize that 20 minute adventure is really all the planet has to offer and there's nothing more but copy pasted ruins and items on it. I really want to love this game but every thing feels so dang vapid once the realization hits and then you can't really play without getting bored until next update and then the cycle begins anew. 

The space travel system and merchant system is pretty fun but ends up suffering from the same issues if you are consistently playing. This game has a real issue with it overstaying it's welcome. You will catch yourself wanting to play and flying around only to lose motivation mid flight realizing you've more than likely already done what ever you're about to heading out to do. The spaceship ruins update was exciting to me until you realize each scrap ship is the same layout as well. The immersion and feeling from the first one felt like they were onto something amazing but that quickly died out after the 10th-11th time. The game suffers extremely hard from repetition until fatigue. 

Base building has the same issue where you will build a beautiful base, but it doesn't really do too much, a.k.a building in minecraft effect. There's so much they could do with random events and have creatures interact with your base or just any kind of interactivity aside from the NPC's you put in place. Subnautica's bases feel substantial while NMS bases feel like an after thought. This effect is compounded by the fact you will get tired of the planet you're on no matter how pretty after at most a few hours due to the previously mentioned lack of variety on planets. 

I am hoping they do a large planet overhaul with proper exploration, biome's, seasons and unique locations worthy of staying on the planet. As it functions now, the main feature of exploration still feels extremely hollow and not worth your time unless you like to just travel and explore without caring about the depth of the game. I've "beaten" (credits roll) the game multiple times and just can't stay hype about it with the main feature being so lackluster.

All in all a solid 6/10 but hard to recommend given it's been 5 years. I've put in around 130 hours since the start and it's rather hard to recall anything about my playthrough's aside from S class ships and some of the oddities that pretty much require a drop, taking the fun out of it. The time sink vs memorable moments is rather drab, this is coming from a Warframe player too, so that should clue you in on how much grind there is. 

TL;DR: Worth a shot on game pass where it's free currently (6/4/21) and seeing if you vibe with the game other wise catch it on sale for 30$. The developer def deserves credit for standing by their product & supporting it but still have a long way to go in terms of content with actual variety & depth. Banal content on each planet you land on will put you off if you're into games with more than surface level entertainment.
Reviews.107717:
I wanted to love this game. I went in and played for 12 hour sessions and very quickly climbed the tech tiers. As I played, I saw all these awesome looking ships and frigates. I built a base up and acquired the exocraft vehicles, the thing I anticipated most. I can say from my experience, I did not have fun. 
	For starters, beginning the game was interesting. Starting on a hazardous planet and fighting to stay alive was a good way to grab my attention and teach me the basic mechanics. Repairing my ship and leaving that planet was rewarding. After I left the planet, I did some exploration and began working on the story objective. I got bored at the point where I had to jump to a planet, place a signal booster for a 7 second cutscene, then leave to go to another planet. 
	As I explored aimlessly, I found a nice mushroom planet with some cool looking luminescent grass. I decided to build a base there and opened up the base building aspect. The base building was very bland. It was only a place for some select machines and production facilities. The main purpose was to eventually produce a lot of units from planetary resources. Once I got bored of the very one dimensional base building system, I started looking into the Exocraft.
These exocraft seemed awesome in concept, but the execution was very disappointing. I enjoy exploration type games that involve vehicles as they really open up the speed you can explore at. The Roamer being my first vehicle that I upgraded fully is the one I have the most experience with. It was interestingly powerful in some cases; wielding a super powerful mining laser that worked quickly and a power scanning system that made tracking specific structures possible. The biggest downside to the vehicles was that they were so irrationally slow. It seriously felt like it was faster to sprint and use my jetpack. It gets worse when you’re driving on a planet with water, since your vehicle will slow down 40% its original speed when a single wheel gets within one foot of a small puddle. The vehicles work better as an upgraded signal booster than an actual car. Also, the mech handles like the worst thing I’ve ever felt.
I’ve lost motivation to continue writing this review. Pretty much, progression in this game feels way too samey. Anything you do unlock that is unique very quickly becomes stale. It’s nice to see the game devs working hard on their new content, but I wish they would have done a better job at making the things you can do more fun.
Reviews.107719:
No Man's Sky has come a long, long, long way from it's launch.

I have played NMS on and off since the day it released. I initially logged about 60+ hours on the base release of NMS; and if this were the same game it was 5 years ago, I don't think I would be able to recommend it.

[b]But[/b]

In the 5 years since release, the developers have continuously supported the game and released updates. They have piled on content and evolved the stuff you can do in the game. The environments have improved, the mechanics have improved, the graphics and sound have improved (multi-tools still feel a bit anemic though...better than on launch..but still not like, bolter from 40k punchy).

You should set expectations for what the core of this game is. It is mostly about exploration. You can set up a base on one planet and keep coming back to it, but I think NMS becomes something special when you start treating it like a game where you are a nomad jumping from place to place.

I also have to give props to the Expeditions update for really helping me 'get' this game. It encouraged me to start fresh (because you have to for an expedition). And that made me embrace the nomadic explorer nature of NMS. It is, bar none, the most fun I have had with NMS since release and pushed me over the edge to really thinking this game has become something special.

from the time and money you save from making ridiculous art updates do this :

"No Man's Sky" is an action exploration RPG game with survival crafting elements to it, yet feels very unfinished and unpolished. Even though I can appreciate the basically infinite world generation aspect of it, the problem is the lack of content inside. With things such as: 

- You only have like 4 enemies in the entire game: 1) Critters scattered about, 2) Robots, 3) Bigger Robots, 4) Space Pirates. The weapon mods for multi-tools are basically worthless as you don't need anything outside of a decent multi-tool to handle 3/4 of the game itself. The multi-tools also don't feel any different from the others. You have Pistols, SMG's, and Rifles. Pistols are small, compact, and often have decent space for utility mods. SMG's are a bit larger than pistols and are able to handle different multi-tool/weapon function mods, but at the lack of as many utility mods-- they're still a bit more expensive than the pistols. Rifles have the most space for multi-tool functionality, as well as pretty hefty asking prices. You also have even less utility mods for enhancing the multi-tool functionality than SMG's. Note: There is plenty of upgrade space for SMG's and Rifles, but pistols seem to be the most unlocked straight from the box. Upgrading for more space for mods on SMG/Rifle multi-tools costs TONS of units, something that doesn't just fall from the sky and it's not recommended to upgrade multi-tools because chances are as soon as you get about a mile down the trail, you'll find a better multi-tool than the one you have and it's plain better to buy new ones with more space and better stats than to waste time upgrading the old multi-tools.

- Farming units is probably one of the most boring and time consuming things to ever grace the world of RPG/Survival Crafting experiences, and there's really nothing you can do to change this.

- Because farming units takes literal days (In Real-time) to accomplish, you're often locked out of getting anything in the game. Gold seems to be a good commodity throughout, as well as the fossils once you find a planet that has them that is. 

- The game does have the ability to choose who you are in the universe, are you the good boy everyone likes? Are you a space faring marauder that ruthlessly attacks freighter/cargo ships to loot the valuables? Do you like one of the races/factions more than the others? Are you some kind of space cop that stops pirates from attacking stations and other space vessels? This part is completely up to the player to figure out and there's no hands being held for it. This I like. 

- For an RPG, you aren't locked to any particular "class", which means there aren't any particular benefits of choosing to be a certain type of character, so it's not quite like Warframe in that regard, but not being locked to a certain character play style gives freedom of choice, until you realize there's really not much choice to be had. You have automatic firing mods, shotgun mods, burst fire mods, sniper-like mods, missile launcher mods, grenade launcher mods, all of which do nothing considering there's still only like 4 enemies in the game and one of those types of enemies are only fought in space in your ship. The different suit mods however DO play a certain role. Some suit mods make you more spacious so you have room to haul a ton of loot around, some give you better abilities for fighting (enhanced damage shielding, better survival stuff, etc). 

- The different ships are what's most intriguing about this title. You have a LOT to choose from: Fighters, Haulers, ship equivalents of a hybrid sedan, freighter ships that act as a mobile base-- so many to choose from, but again, you won't be able to afford 99% of them, so there's no point in bothering. They're just there to look shiny in a display case outside your budget so you can continue to flail about with trying to farm units until you give up because you've been at it for 3-4 hours and still don't even have half the amount needed. 

- The frieghter ships you can get are interesting in that you now have your own fleet to command, complete with a crew to control and cargo space. You also gain access to different "quests" which can yield different resources, some of which are very rare and I believe some of which are only collected during those salvage missions. The problem with the freighter quests are that 1) It takes HOURS upon HOURS of real time, 2) The cost of the journey isn't exactly cheap either, and 3) You could always get bummed out on RNG. Freighters in particular have TONS of storage space, where you can load in thousands of resources and haul that precious cargo from here to there to find good asking prices for selling. The problem is that freighters themselves do not have a lot of space for MULTIPLE goods-- I've found that the Hauler ships of similar level/class actually have more space. Why is a ship the size of a comparative SUV carrying more than a flying fortress? The freighter is almost just good for having a few landing pads for Haulers. 

- The graphics are GORGEOUS-- when they work. If you build a fairly large base, the framerate tanks considerably. If you have a lot of dug out holes, the framerate tanks. 

- Replayability is basically nonexistent because the game is infinitely playable on one character. There's no need to create new characters in this game. Any kinds of faction issues can be resolved through quests or good Samaritan stuff, like saving a faction's freighter from pirates and such. 

Overall, this game really needs work. It feels like a gigantic sandbox with nothing but sand in it. There's really very little to do even with all of those updates and it still feels unpolished. Granted this is leagues above where it started at a few years ago, but the game still has things to add. Despite the negative connotation, it's very enjoyable to play and has great potential for better things. I hope Hello Games continues to improve on it and I will update my review periodically as it goes on. I know I only have ~30 hours so far, but I have about 4x as much on my PS4. So far, I give it 7/10 and I do recommend it to others.

I've had this game from it's initial launch. I remember very clearly begging my parents to let me pre-order it the night before the game's release. They eventually let me and all I had to do was wait in pure excitement. Quintillions of places to go in this absolutely massive universe, with a mix of existing elements and compounds plus made up sciencey looking stuff? What's not to love. Well, it turns out there was a lot not to love...

For the first part, a mistake made by me. Being young and not understanding how PCs work, my old as hell HP laptop was not going to run this game, not even close. So my disappointment when I download it and spend 2 hours trying to boot the game, each time watching it fail to even show up on the screen, just make noises, was a lot. I'd hyped myself up so much for this game and to find I won't get to experience it at all felt terrible. My friend was going to get the game but we agreed to see me play it first before we both try and play together (an unknowingly smart decision on our part). My hopes had been crushed before even seeing the title screen, but after Googling it, it seemed I wasn't alone. I have a vivid memory of reading an article saying that even the recommended specs weren't actually good enough for it, the game was already on a very steep decline. Furthermore, weeks and weeks later, my idiot self then found out about the Steam refund system (ironically through another article about this "game"). It was already much too late to refund it and get my wasted £40 back.

A few years passed and I'd moved on from that complete disappointment of a game, or so I thought. I eventually built the PC I use today and in my sheer excitement I remembered that long forgotten tragedy that I know I can now run. So I download it and start playing (this was still pre Next update, but not long before it). I finally load onto a planet and see my ruined ship for the first time and I will admit, that made me incredibly happy. It was short lived as I quickly found the game's main flaw, in my opinion; its terribly tedious grinding. Planets started to look the same, just big circles with some wacky colours, an environmental problem and resources so I could take off and move to the next wacky coloured toxic mess. The story felt like it was headed somewhere but somehow never felt like it was progressing. The most interesting part of playing to me was the added portals that each space station had and that your home base could have built. The goddamn fast travel system was more interesting than the actual game and even then I was quickly disappointed to find my ship must've come through the portal with me because there it was, docked on a landing pad! After a while of searching the basically infinite cosmos for any sign of fun, I stopped and uninstalled. I would have to wait for someone to play with.

That day came. A friend of mine saw the game (post Next update) and wanted to try it out. The spark of interest was back with the exciting prospect of playing with other people. We'd both downloaded and booted up, made a session to play in and started. We didn't start together though, we had to work our way towards travelling to each other, a feature I actually quite like the idea of however it should be an option to start on the same planet. We played for maybe 10-15 hours in total before we both agreed there wasn't something quite right about this game. Luckily he had gotten Star Citizen, which encouraged me to also hop onto Star Citizen. I can barely run SC, playing, at best, at 30 FPS (the average was much lower) but the experience that space sim offered was infinitely better than what No Man's Sky gave me. Sure, SC is still very much in development with no real release date on the horizon, but it was easily better an No Man's Sky; an early access game that was advertised as a full release title, priced as a full release title, and basically scammed young me.

I've tried to go back to this game, several times. Each time I find myself thinking that there's something missing. Something they could've done that would make it so much better. It's definitely incredibly subjective to think that but that's what reviews are. I've even now dipped my toes in Elite Dangerous' gameplay and that was still way better than anything No Man's Sky has given me. I genuinely don't think I could get into this game, not as much as the other 2 space sims I've mentioned. If you want a game where you get to play as a person living in a future in the cosmos (assuming you have a beefy enough computer), play SC. The attention to detail in that game is genuinely remarkable and, even though its scale currently is relatively tiny to the other games I've mentioned, it still feels huge. If you want a space sim for vehicles and a massive incomprehensible size, get Elite Dangerous. A 1:1 scale of the Milky Way, set in a future a thousand or so years away, with massive variety in vehicles and stars and pathways and planets and even home itself. I really hope they fix Odyssey because on-foot gameplay is the only feature I think is seriously missing from Elite, to make it that much more brilliant of a space exploration.

No Man's Sky has only one good quality. That is the fact it is a massive warning to anyone who hypes themselves up about a game, to anyone who thinks pre-ordering games is a good idea, and to anyone that lets their excitement of the mere concept of the game be better than what the actual game turns out to be. Reviews.107842:
No Man's Sky

What can I say that hasn't been said about this game. From its highs and its lows, it is a journey I never want to forget. I've followed this game since its launch, grown disappointed with the lackluster launch, like everyone was. But only until 4 years later did I get it, mostly because now I have the hardware to run it. But this game is an enigma. Should I call it beautifully "designed" but all the worlds were not made by a developers hand, they were created by an AI designed to create them. So, maybe I should be impressed at the code work done to create worlds so beautiful. 

This game is best enjoyed at whatever pace you deem comfortable, with whatever playstyle suits you. You could be a trader, travelling the universe to find the most expensive items. You could be a survivalist, toughing it out in the most deadly of locations. Or you could play as a galactic photographer, taking pictures across the universe. I enjoy this sort of play. The game is an open canvas for you to paint whichever way you please. 

Now, as much as I go on about the perfection and beauty of this title. I will say, it has some flaws. Carrying over from the games earlier days, it has some bugs, still. some very, very annoying bugs that could completely break your game that still haven't been patched. And another problem that has affected me the most. Now, I do enjoy a survival game, especially titles like Minecraft, Subnautica, and Starbound. These titles are good examples of a survival game, with the material gathering and the crafting and whatever. But with this, it honestly just feels too tedious starting out, especially getting the funds to buy a ship. The only reason I could buy ships is from a rich player just randomly dropping ship parts worth 250 mil on my head. One final criticism. There needs to just be.. more, I guess. It doesn't feel like what you do impacts anyone outside of some text. There should be actual factions to join, to be able to go to, something akin to Fallout's factions. some organizations that level up as you do radiant quests isn't good enough. I want to make connections to characters outside of the (surprisingly good) story.

But I digress. No Man's Sky is not a game for everyone, I will say that. But it very much has found a special place in mine and many others hearts, the ones that continue to explore the universe for something we find interesting. Is that enough for people? Of course. Even with my criticisms, I'm satisfied with the experience I came out with, but still, it could use just a little more features. 

9.5/10 Thank you Sean Murray and Hello Games.

Reviews.107973:
HIGH EFFORT REVIEW
With the release of the Prisms update, I thought it was time to chime in with a review with 200+ hours in the game and hundreds more hopefully in the future. SO, let us get into the in-depth review.

GAME PLAY
There is such a vast amount to explore and do in NMS. You often hear past reviews say that the Universe is huge, but with nothing to do, lack of uniqueness and variety. While I can agree to that to an extent, this is becoming more and more untrue as Hello Games pushes out more updates. The sheer amount of content that has been released from Desolation, Origins, Next Generation, Companions, Expeditions, and now Prisms, has shown Hello Games is dedicated to building this “empty universe” into something where everyone can find a home.

NMS provides such a wide array of things like combat, exploration/discovery, cooking, companion collecting, etc.… Some of the criticisms I hear is that there is a lot of to do but it does not have the depth that some players seek. I think that is a completely valid criticism, but I have no doubt that more content will be added that will refine and expand these systems.

I can admit that in the later game, some people will have the urge to automate things such as mining and accrue billions of credits like me. This can cause certain mechanics like exocrafts to fall by the wayside since they are not “optimal”. We could all discuss solutions to this, but the reality is that people want to min/max everything and have the most optimized gameplay. I provide solutions to this under “THE FUTURE OF NMS?”

AUDIO
This section is probably going to be one of the most important to me. A good soundtrack and sound effects are CRITICAL for a game like this. You want the sound design to capture the sheer vastness of space, the emptiness of space, the mystery of the unknown, and the terror of what lies beyond the unknown. 
65daysofstatic met this challenge head on and obliterated it.

For all the people that do not know, 65DOS created the NMS soundtrack and have had experience in this type of music for over a decade (Everyone should give their album “Wild Light” a listen). What makes this soundtrack different from all the others is that it is procedurally generated music. With the vast number of experiences, you will have in NMS, it makes since that the game needs a wide variety of sounds to fit those experiences. In my opinion, I think this was the best solution and 65DOS was the only band that could accomplish it. The feeling of when you land on a world type you have never seen, and the music becomes more bombastic to reflect the discovery and wonder of that world is unmatched. I still remember getting chills down my spine the first time I stepped onto a Hyperborean Planet and the crescendo hit. I would highly recommend reading some articles or videos to expand on how they did this, it is so impressive.

On to the dialog/voice acting… For the species within the NMS universe (Gek, Korvax, Vy’Keen, Travelers, and Anomaly), I think that the audio for them was well matched. Gek is easily my favorite voicing and fits them so well. As Paul Weir said in an interview, the voice acting is not procedurally generated. I assume its due to the unique languages that were created and having to match those up to actual sounds all the time. I think there is room for improvement for the range of words or “noises” the intelligent species can make and slowly start matching those with the actual language of the species. It is a tall task but would be insane for players to hear and understand it.

On to the sound effects… This is where I become less impressed and think there needs to be some refining and tweaking done. While I love certain sound effects like a shuttle landing, I cannot stand other ones like refiner noises. I absolutely detest the portable refiner noise; it haunts my nightmares to this day. For experienced players, in my early play through I would refine viscous fluids to nanites, around 120k worth. This takes a long time, and the portable refiner sound gets to me and becomes the soundtrack to my life. I would pay for a DLC to change just this…

Okay, done with my rant on refiner sounds. The rest of the SFX is decent. I think that NMS would benefit greatly from tweaking explosion, weapon, ship sounds. This could be in the form of using more plangent and low-pitched sounds in space. A perfect example of this is space travel in the game “Elite Dangerous”. That game really makes you feel the vastness and terror of open space. Having more of a deep rattle or dull echo from the haul from the vacuum of space would add a lot of immersion. The same can be said about explosions in space or on a planet. I want to feel the rattle in my bones when a geology cannon goes off besides me. This is the perfect opportunity to tweak this due to the Prisms update including more detailed asteroid explosions. I want to feel the risk and destructions of destroying these asteroid belts.

STORY
While I enjoy the story itself and I think that there is a lot of potential for it, it can fall short. For an example, I did not follow the main story line for the first 80+ hours and just explored and got rich. I think this is a double-edged sword because you can make your own decisions. You can go build a cabin in a Lush Planet and retire rich and not know the story or lead a life of exploration and discovery. I love that there are those options. But, if there is going to be those options, I would love for richer universe information, side stories, more information on the history of these species, long-lost civilizations that the Gek traded into poverty because they are the master race species (Gek is the true master race). 

IS IT WORTH?
Absolutely. Right now, it is 50% off. Just get it, get it if it is full price. 

THE FUTURE OF NMS?
Who knows? The pace of Hello Games shows us that there will absolutely be more content, and they are going full steam ahead in 2021. Below are some bullet points on what I think Hello Games could look at if they ever come across this post to summarize my suggestions from the review.

•	Create more content for currency system. As someone who has billions of units, I only use it for buying ships and scrapping them to get modules. This could be done in the form of customization of exosuits and starships like wing design, color, etc.… It would be 100,000,000 units to change color, we need a unit sink for further customization or expansion of features to deter burnout of long-term players.


•	Expand on side story or individual species backstories/history. Who is the leader of the Gek? A cool addition would be if we achieved the “Trade-Lord” title and were able to meet high ranking Gek. Or if we had a hostile relationship with the Vy’keen, we could meet them that way. It is a tall task, just would be cool for lore purposes after the main story line. OR even a “glitch” that could introduce other species or characters that could play on the whole concept of the collecting the stabilized reality glitches. There is an infinite amount of growth for a story like this and it seems like Hello Games set it up that way to allow the expansion of these paths.

This game has been an amazing journey and I can’t wait to see what is next on the journey to the center of the universe. Knowing all of this, I recognize Hello Games is a company and working so many years on FREE updates, I would be totally on board for a huge DLC. I know people are always hesitant to pay for DLC, but Hello Games has shown time and time again their commitment to improving on their short comings and I would 100% be on board for paying for a DLC. Think about the massive amount of content they have provided over the years? Now imagine it if they had additional funds? The content of the DLC has the potential to dwarf all previous content and give NMS a second wind and much needed funds for future projects.

Thanks for the hundreds of hours of fun Hello Games.

No Man's Sky started out as a gimmick rather than a game: a tech demo showing users the capabilities of procedural generation without much depth. Over the years, large amounts of content have been added to the game and the game can finally be presented as a "game"

This game has many shortcomings. 
- The flora and fauna you encounter gets repetitive. The more planets you visit, the more you realize that especially fauna are made up out of a set number of variables. For example, many planets will have creatures that look like bipedal deer. Some planets have bioluminescent flora, but the pattern in which the bioluminescence exhibits itself is the same - even on planets hundreds of lightyears apart from each other
- The lore has so many gaps and unknowns that it can barely be called lore. When you first start out the game, you feel like you've been dropped into a story with lore that goes deeper than Star Wars or Halo go. Once you finish the main storyline (if we can call it that), you realize that 80% of the intel, logs and lore have no significance to playing the game whatsoever.
- To cite another review: No Man's Sky is still a walking and gathering simulation. It should be noted that, once you have completed the main storyline, have the starship you want and a nice freighter, money barely serves any purpose anymore. The only point of the game at that point is exploring planet after planet and maybe building a base on one you think looks pretty.

There are also many positives, though:
- The story is told in a unique way
- Building a pretty and useful base feels rewarding
- It's hard to resist the urge to visit a planet that looks promising, curious or just pretty.
- and last but certainly not least: PLAYING TOGETHER IS FUN

Seriously. Play this game with a friend. Build an awesome base together on a cool planet you discovered together.

I will recommend this game. Why? Simply because, despite its shortcomings, I enjoyed the game and I still do. And I think many others will, too.

Just completed a new game in Expedition mode.

Expeditions provide a set of milestones with massive rewards, that help speed up a new game and  give an overall goal and navigate the humongous amount of content NMS provide. The reward of this expedition was an S-Rank frigate, part of the auxiliary fleet of your freighter, the reward is accessible to all saves through the anomaly.

Multiplayer: The multiplayer is a lot more stable than it used to be, framerates are still choppy, and sometimes other player bases don't spawn in. By calling the anomaly in space, you can meet other players and complete quest together for a reward. Overall this mode has become playable to me.

Stability: Just one crash in about 10 hours of play. I would consider it stable.

Content: There are systems upon systems in this game in immense procedurally generated galaxies. Base building, exploration, reseacrch, factions. 150h in and I still have things to do. I won't list them in detail here.

Resources: The first thing I do with a new save is to use a portal to go to a base another player provide. Going to bases that mark either an high class crashed ship, a huge refinery to sell resources for currency or sources of nanite, it's a nice way to have credits in case you come across an high class ship you want to buy in a station.

Art style: The procedural generation is AMAZING. Ice planets, paradise worlds, death worlds, even HEXAGONAL worlds. Each of them with procedurally generated minerals, plants and animals, some of them hilarious and/or exotic. I just like to jump from system to system and look what the procedural generation has in store for me.

Story: Story is usually a weak point in an open world procedurally generated game. The thing I love the most about the story in NMS is the mystery of it all unravelling and the sheer beauty of the places where those mysteries are revealed.

Conclusions: NMS is a great game. I like huge games where I can explore, build, discover the game system and more, and NMS provide this in spades. I'll keep playing it for a long time, even just towitness a sunset on a moon around a giant with large rings.

This'll be a first for me. Originally marked this as a recommend because my game was relatively stable. Since Expeditions released though, so many bugs have been introduced that it's more of a chore than a game.

No Man's Sky was ok while I ignored the storyline and did my own thing, but delivered an underwhelming sense of "is that it?" on completion of the major quests.
After a while there is simply no reason to do anything because nothing you do has any real impact on the universe you inhabit.

You've seen the four planet types. You've fought space pirates for the 1000000th time with your "fighter" ship. You've attempted to 100% scan the fauna on a planet (which inevitably doesn't fully spawn). Your base staff are useless and now do nothing. Credits and nanites are now over-flowing and given to you like trash, but there's not much to do with them, as your inventory has long since filled up. More storage? .. not an option. Why would you need more than 10 boxes in an infinite galaxy? (some items only stack to 20.. urgh)
Quicksilver (given for missions at the anomaly) is also in short supply and will gain you nothing that impactful.
Rewards for later added missions will grant you worse ships than the one you currently have.

Similar to Fallout 4 on its release, No Man's Sky suffers from a real lack of direction, which is perhaps to be expected from a procedurally-generated world, with very little of interest inserted, and plenty of broken quests.
Quests are mostly of the fetch variety, granting you underwhelming rewards for underwhelming quests. As I mentioned, bugs are frequent, and now seem to be regularly introduced. Everything just feels static with the exception of the mountain of unfixed bugs.
I heard someone refer to this game as a "proof of concept masquerading as a game" and I think that person nailed it.

My hours are high because alt-tabbing would crash to desktop/bluescreen and restarting the game would force me to load twice because the textures rarely load on the first opening, so I'd just leave it on and avoid the twenty hour opening space graphics and restart.

If you do get this, get it on sale, No Man's Sky has little to do, and even less to say, but sometimes the sunsets can be kind of pretty.

Reviews.114442:
Often crashes, bugs, horrible user interface that needs tons of QoL improvement. Needlessly convoluted gameplay mechanics, like the lack of manual save without crafting the beacons or sitting in a ship. And lack of custom markers without crafting them - absolutely ridiculous, it's an exploration game! You can wander around for hours, but then the game crashes and you're fucked because you didn't summon your ship to save in it or build a save beacon. 

Pretty planets, but as it's all procedurally generated, the illusion of fresh content vanes fast. Mineral and fauna structures are often repeated. Animals fare a bit better, and they range from decent to abominations from Spore. I've had moments where I was genuinely interested in an animal, then there were moments when I said "that's literally just a dinosaur", and then there were couple moments where the animal looked so awful and goofy it broke the immersion. 
And this is why I will take a game with handcrafted content anyday over this autogenerated content, especially complex stuff like animals. 

Ship controls are garbage, and they pilot more like jet planes than spaceships - you don't even have vertical and horizontal thrusters. Free look is useless as unholding the button doesn't snap you back to default view, instead it points the ship to where you were looking. Horrid design. Space combat is pretty easy, the only difficulty are the bad ship controls.

Base building can be fun, but certain things are incredibly annoying to place, especially the goddamn landing pad. Building camera is rather useless, as you can't even zoom in or out and it's honestly easier to build from first person. 

It often feels like I'm fighting the game instead of enjoying it, especially in the first few hours. Charge this, charge that, now mine this and harvest that - it's chaotic and makes for some bad initial impressions, especially when your first planed is toxic or irradiated and you're constantly on the run to survive with barely any room to relax. Because you don't have a ship, you can't even save for about half an hour into the game.

I won't deny I've had my fun, but the bugs, crashes and bad performance (especially in the Anomaly station) don't give me a big desire to continue playing. Game has potential and it has come far from what it used to be in 2016, so I gotta hand it to devs for sticking through and actually improving it. But in its current state, I don't feel like playing it any more. 

I will wait for Elite Dangerous: Odyssey to come out. It won't have atmospheric planets with full ecosystems like NMS does, but I know it will work far better, UI will be functional and simpler and the gameplay will be more satisfactory than this.

Edit as of June 2021: yeah the last part didn't age well at all

I'll give an "overall impression" and then dissect it a bit more after, giving some of the bugs and "feature fixes" I think they should implement. I'll edit this to add other notes as I remember them, if I do, but I think I got most of it this first time.

Overall, I love it! I'm addicted. The gameplay is very enjoyable, not too difficult to learn, and no small number of people have hundreds, even thousands of hours of time invested in it. It's a quasi-sandbox type of game with many aspects of gameplay in common with Minecraft, but much, much better graphics and 3D navigation. It also has actual storylines, or "paths", which you can either follow or ignore as per your preference. There are some things you won't become privy to or acquire if you don't do "The Atlas Path" the first time around, but once you do it to a certain point, you can quit if you want to.

As far as technical issues go, there are a number of features that need improvement. But check out its update history - it's a work in progress, and updates are relatively frequent. So it's still in pretty active development, and the improvements are usually fairly noteworthy.

One of the downs is the repetitiveness. The dialog of NPCs is recycled over and over and over, and some of them will present you with offers or situations that you've already dealt with. For instance, when you're building up your base. Every space station has a little room where the beings there will offer to work for you, and say it was "destined" or "already paid for", even though you've had one of them from another station already working for you for in-game centuries. I'd rather they stop making that offer once you've hired one of them, because it really wrecks the suspension of disbelief that makes for the best gameplay. Overall, they have only a small number of scripts for each type of being to rehash when you encounter them - it's bearable, but it would be so much better if they could increase the NPC's repertoire a bit.

Also, after awhile, you get to feeling like all of the creatures on all of the worlds are virtually the same. There is some small amount of variety from planet to planet, but, for instance, all hyper-radioactive worlds will have beasts the same general "shape" as the beasts on all other hyper-radioactive worlds, and virtually all of the creatures on all of the worlds make the same exact sounds.

Battles are also interesting. They try to pretty much "force" you into dogfights with few convenient ways of opting-out if you're not interested, primarily by disabling your escape mechanisms once the "hostile subspace scan" has started, or not allowing you to re-board your freighter once a 'battle' is in progress. You can come out of subspace into the middle of a battle in-progress, and about the only way out is to warp to another system. Very inconvenient.

When you're in the mood for a space battle, though, it's not too shabby. It's not real easy to get killed, and your hits seem to inflict almost fatal damage every time - it's a bit of a gravy train, so if you like challenging battles, it's not that challenging. I don't play for the battles, though, so that doesn't bother me. But for those who like to shoot it out with a high risk of death or injury, you may be left disappointed.

Derelict freighters are also interesting ways to earn lots of money (you can get lots of tainted metal, which can be converted to nanites, one of the most useful currencies of the game as far as buying upgrades and the like). They're often repetitive, but as long as you don't visit them in the same system too often, they manage to have enough variety to keep it somewhat fresh. If you don't like fighting the little crab critters that shoot plasma from their mouths, run or teleport to the primary airlock and step outside for a few and they'll be gone when you get back. It's a bit of a cheat, but for me, if I had to fight as many of them as they sometimes put there, I just wouldn't bother with the derelicts to begin with. I'd rather 'cheat' a little and enjoy the game more than to miss out entirely on that feature.

Be careful when using your pulse drive to approach craft such as your freighter. If you don't stop before you get there, you could end up "inside" the ship, stuck in its innards. If you find yourself in that situation, you don't have to close the game or anything - just use the galaxy map to warp to a nearby system and then warp back again. Another bug I hope they'll work out sometime soon.

I may add to this as I think of other bugs I forgot to mention, but those are the important ones. If you're expecting perfection right out of the box, you might want to wait a bit. But if the things I mentioned don't sound too off-putting to you, give it a go! It's addictive, and I quite enjoy it!

Edit: Ah, yes. The medium & large refiners. For some reason, they occasionally "eat" the contents of the hopper you'd put into them  for refining. I don't know what causes it or how to avoid it. If you stay in the refiner/hopper screen while its refining and don't leave, you're usually okay, but "babysitting" the things isn't exactly a constructive use of time. The bug has been around for awhile, and they really need to fix it soon. But I don't know if they will. If you only have one ingredient to refine, you might want to stick with the "portable refiners" - they require fuel unlike the medium/large refiners, but never eat the inventory.

[b] TLDR the overall balance of the game feels clumsy, if not completely broken [/b]

Even if the game is much more complete nowadays, one "problem" still remains, and for me it's the weak point of the game, by far : the balance of the game.

Example : I just reached the center of Euclid today in permadeath, which is theoritically the hardest achievement, and...  well that was extremely easy.
That was my second run, my first one ended because I killed myself in one shot with my plasma cannon (the irony, the only things that can kill you are explosive weapons, that only you can use, and fall damage. So the biggest danger... is yourself).

But what about the other dangers ?
[b] Space battle : [/b]

Any space battle can literally be won with the very first ship you get, with the default upgrades, it takes a bit of skill but it can be done (with rocket launcher). 
Even if you were a very bad pilot you can still stock up resources to instantly recharge your ship's shield. 
Every ship you destroy will drop something to instantly recharge your ship's shield (well, no need to recharge it yourself then...).
Enemies will do way less damages than you (I think your ship takes artificially 3 times less damages that what you can inflict).
Any ship you buy with better stats, any combat upgrades, are only here to provide a comfort for space battle.

[b] Ground battle : [/b]

First, most ground battles can be avoided. 
Some planets will have "predators", that will move as fast as slugs, and you'll get a big red warning if they come too close. I think I got hit only once in the 50+ hours it took me to reach the center, and of course it barely scratched my shield (and permadeath has [b] increased [/b] damages!)
There are also sentinels, here to guard planets from players (destroying flora and fauna). Well they do a very bad job
If you destroy something and a sentinel come, just stop and it will scan you and go away.
You can even go a bit further and destroy stuff behind it, like that you can move it away from you (it will just move were the thing was destroyed, with a sad look in his eye)
On some planet the difficulty is harder, sentinels attack you on sight. Problem is, after several shield upgrades, it will take a huge time for them to completely destroy your shield
And even then, as usual in this game, there is a way to counter it
When a sentinel spot you, it will spawn 2 other sentinels. Now you could just escape, but what if you just want to stay were you are? Well you can, just destroy 2 sentinels, let one "alive", and it will never call for reinforcements (20 IQ exploit). After that you can build an entire base on the planet, literally anything except going afk should be fine, while the poor sentinel will shoot you with its airsoft gun.

[b] Extreme weathers : [/b]

After literally 2 hours max, you'll be able to buy a huge supply of batteries and life support gels for barely nothing. With that you can survive on any planet in the game, period... And after you get S class modules, storms will just be (good looking) visual effects.

[b] What about nanites and money making? [/b]

To get millions in the first few hours, just find a planet with ancient bones. You'll be able to make something like 20 millions/hour.
To make a lot of nanites, you can go in a spacestation and buy then scrap every ship with a class equal or above to B.
You'll get modules that you can sell for nanites. With that, you can make even more money (sell scraps in the right space stations, use expension storages on a ship the sell it for a huge price...) and about 20-30k nanites/hour (in 2 hours you have enough to buy every upgrades for your suit, multitool, and ship. yay).

Now the biggest problem is that those are not glitch/exploit at all, they are [b] intended [/b] ways from the devs.
Keep in mind that I'm ok with the game being easy in normal mode, but here [b] the game feels extremely easy in the hardest mode possible [/b].

So why do I recommend it then? Well if you're not searching for a challenging game, at all, if you don't mind playing a game that feels like one big exploit, then it's a great game. This is, for me, the best exploration game that exists as of today. It's really a unique experience, being able to discover new planets, each time a different atmosphere, the complete freedom of building everywhere, on every planet. I think this game really shines in that aspect. 
And even if you don't really need to do it, there are a lot of things to do, lots of missions, building a base, searching for better ship, planet with specific characteristics, going to the center of the galaxy, going to a specific galaxy, unlocking everything, visiting other player creations etc.

No Man's Sky is a chill survival exploration game. Literally, you can start on a sub-zero planet and start to freeze to death. If only your scanner wasn't broken when you started, then you could easily find sodium to power up your hazard protection systems and fend off impending hypothermia.

Your journey begins.

Mining survival resources with your trusty multi-tool (which, by the way, also needs to be charged up with resources) you should soon reach a point where you aren't about to freeze to death or expire from lack of charge in the old life support system.

The sentinels. Servants of a mysterious and omniscient entity known as ATLAS, they seek out disturbances to the planets that they patrol. One of them may have already been alerted by the energy signature of your mining beam. If they believe that you present a continuing threat with your resource gathering, they will initiate suppression measures. You can run, or you can fight, but continued aggression will provoke an ever-stronger response from the sentinels. Only when you have eluded their sensors for a long enough time will they stop their pursuit.

Did I forget to mention that there are also bloodthirsty animals and toxic plants? Must have slipped my mind, sorry.

When you finally reach your starship and hop into the cockpit, I hope you have picked up some ferrite dust, oxygen, carbon and di-hydrogen, because you're going to need to hop back out and do some repairs before you can take off.

It sounds like a lot, and it is, but once you've played through the start of the game a few times you'll be experienced enough to know how to speed through that initial part and get to the good stuff.

Or, you can put that experience to use during one of the time-limited expeditions, which give you a lot of what you need to get started right off the bat, but there's no tutorial beyond what you can read in the guide. After the expedition is over, you'll be able to claim expedition rewards at the Space Anomaly in every subsequent game that you start, and you'll be able to continue the expedition save in Normal mode, which is one of the easiest difficulty settings.

You can build your own base aboard a capital ship, which is the nerve centre of your own fleet expeditions, which bring back profits from trading, mineral from mining, and so on. This base will be reconstructed in the event that you trade in your current capital ship for a newer model. Or, if you like the smell of fresh air, you can construct bases freely on any planet that you encounter, assuming that you survive the hostile elements that prevail on some worlds. There are some paradise worlds out there if that's what you're searching for, you just have to keep looking.

Reviews.138095:
Started playing around the time that NEXT came out. I cannot speak for the game's apparent low quality around the time of its original release as a result. That being said, the game as it exists now is quite astonishing; an effective combination of crafting and resource gathering games like Minecraft and a more casualised take on space exploration games like Elite Dangerous. Keep in mind that you could love both of those games and still find little to love here; however, the same goes both ways, and the game stands out enough as its own creature that I can't help but recommend it to anyone who's even vaguely interested. The procedurally-generated worlds are a sight to behold, and while the story is somewhat barebones, it is still an incredibly interesting and enthralling ride. There's something here for everyone; crafting, trading, building, dogfights, the list goes on.

My only complaint is that the game is still quite buggy (excusable considering the game's scope and small dev team), but I'm confident that the game will continue to grow and stabilise as it's been shown that Hello Games have a vested interest in improving and adding to their product in an ongoing fashion.

tl;dr: If you're looking for a chilled out, exploration-based experience with some awesome and chilling moments in S P A C E, this will be right up your alley. Maybe just wait for it to go on sale, until the game's bugs are more ironed-out.

EDIT: I'm now a significant number of hours deeper into No Man's Sky and I can confidently state that a lot of the issues I was having with bugs have been ironed out. The game is much more stable now and has had numerous quality-of-life updates, and that's saying nothing of the free updates that have continued to roll out. It's especially great with friends! In my opinion the most notable changes since I originally published this review are the addition of derelict freighters that you can land on and explore, the overhaul to the game's cave systems and planet terrain generation, and the recently-added Expeditions mode. This game is now a shining pinnacle of its genre and it deserves to be played by anybody with even a passing interest.

No Man's Sky has come a long way since its full release, but sadly it has a lot of bugs and some poor design choices.

I want to start off with the most positive thing I've found about the game so far.  You can eventually explore any planet or moon that you can see.  Any at all.  It may take a while to get there, but you can.  There's not one place on one planet I haven't been able to go so far.  I think you'll be able to go anywhere, but will need better gear to survive the harsher environments.  That's all great, kind of amazing they've done this using procedural generation so it's different for each planet.

It has multiplayer as long as everyone's in the same game mode (there are 4 right now) but mission progress is not shared and if you die you may not spawn near your pals.  You can also bump into other players, guaranteed in some areas, but it's very unlikely you'll see anyone randomly since the universe is so vast.  It's too bad there's not more going on there.

The planets look decent from a distance, some border on great, but once you get on the surface their contents are often far too similar.  I expected some snow, rain, and wind but I haven't seen any weather yet.  Yeah, it gets cold, or hot, on some planets but I've never seen a drop of rain, or a snowflake in about 25 hours of play.

It's sad because those first few hours of gameplay are great.  The first time you get your ship up into space, the first time you go to land on a planet, when you start to find new things, and the first time you bump into the NPCs it's so cool, and feels great.  Then you see the blocky clouds, the poor terrain pop-in, the same everywhere grass, the similar flora and fauna, the identical space stations, same six or seven buildings repeated on numerous planets.  It's sad because in the back of your mind you know what it should be, and how it should feel, but it just falls flat.  And then the glitches start, and the grind sets in.

So far for glitches I've seen nothing that's absolutely game breaking.  I've only crashed once, but I have experienced issues where my mouse isn't recognized properly and I have to alt-tab out and back in to get it to work correctly.  I've had trouble with my ships glitching and instead of flying forward they go into some strange forward and back loop where they kind of hover while on planets.  Several other things, too, but again - nothing that breaks the game (except that one crash).  I've heard of others having way more issues than I've had, so don't expect it to be smooth sailing.  Terrain and flora pop in way too close, practically on top of me sometimes, and actually on top of me occasionally.  Not good if you've got a dangerous plant popping in under your feet.  There's a mod to help with it, thank goodness, but it's not perfect.  Hopefully this will be addressed.  Numerous quests are broken, as is base storage.  Sometimes items get stuck and won't transfer to your inventory from storage.

The few dangerous critters you may run into are generally not too aggressive on the normal game difficulty, at least early on, and the sentinels are a joke in some places, but they vary in number and hostility from planet to planet.  Some creatures will also attack you on sight, but they're fairly rare.

Graphics vary, some things are great, some not.  Too many odd filters, glows, blurry textures and blurry text, when you shut most of that off the game starts to look really good, but you have to use mods to fix a lot of it.  It's a shame, because what we were shown is not what we got, even with a few mods tweaking it to look a bit better.  The one place I find the graphics really shine is in the NPCs that you meet.  They all look pretty good, and there's a fair bit of variety even though everyone from each race is always exactly the same size and shape.  I think a lot of work went into each race.  This opens up more as you go farther in the game, you run into some interesting specimens from each species.

There are a decent variety of ships, ways to build a base, and upgrades for your ship and gear.  Certain building options are clunky, but overall it's functional and not too annoying.

There are lots of things to go explore, which is kinda the point, but it often boils down to gather, craft, refuel, travel, repeat.  Luckily once you figure out what fuels you need you can stockpile a bit, but you have limited inventory in the beginning.  It takes a while to either get a bigger ship, or upgrade your exosuit storage.  Despite that, you can fully upgrade the suit before you ever leave the first planet, if you really want to spend that long on one rock.  Once you get the hang of it things get better.  You learn how to travel faster, or more efficiently.  Things open up after the first few hours.

Another of my big complaints is how storage is an issue, and there's an early-game struggle to get more inventory space even though the per-stack limits were raised recently that's not the real issue.  The problem is that there are a large variety of items you will want to hang on to, and you simply have no room to do that.  it's not that hard to expand but it does take time and/or units (No Man's Sky Currency) and some players max that out on the first few planets.  It's possible to grind it out to the max without leaving the first planet, so I'm told, but I don't have the patience to do that.

That's the biggest issue with the game is this.  Tedium.  A lot of very repetitive tasks.  Harvesting is dull but seems to be a huge focus of the game.  Harvesting tool upgrades exist, but I slotted a few, and even put them next to each other for whatever hidden synergy that gives you.  Instead of 40 damage, I now do a whopping 42 damage while mining.  That does not speed it up at all.  Luckily you can eventually build things to harvest for you, significantly cutting down on the grind, but it's a grind to get to that point.  More and more becomes automated as time goes on, and you can expand your base, or bases.  You can get multiple ships, and there's quite a variety.  Some are vastly better than others.

There's a lot of other stuff that feels like a grind, too, but it's discovering more planets, and more of the story, that will keep most of us going.

The story - so far it's actually interesting.  Not great, but I haven't looked anything up online so I'm guessing, and discovering, and that's where this game shines.  You can go anywhere, dig anywhere, build pretty much anywhere.  Freedom.  You can harvest only the bare minimum and focus on exploring.  You can build huge bases.  You can fight enemy pirates (though space combat and ship controls are kinda meh), and even some larger ship combat takes place later on.  Eventually you unlock different missions.  The game is huge, and you're free to explore as much, or little, as you want.

Despite the gripes I have with the game my final verdict is that I do recommend No Man's Sky.  I recently discovered a few things that made me change this review to a more positive one, and I feel like Hello Games are going to keep working to improve the game and fix the bugs.

That brings me to my last point, and it's about the price.  I really don't feel like the game is worth the current price because it still feels unfinished, there are bugs, broken quests, and graphics issues that need to be addressed.  Many of these issues were brought up more than a year ago, so should have been fixed a long time ago.

Anyway, as of Sept 12, 2019 No Man's Sky costs $66.49.  If it were priced at around $40.00 more people would pick it up.  I know I waited for a decent sale before I grabbed it and I'm waiting for another one before I buy it for a gift, or recommend anyone else pick it up.  Maybe once they fix everything it'll be worth the full price, but not when you have to re-start the game or use mods to fix things that shouldn't be broken in the first place.

Man, i was mad.

Now let's skip to today. I gotta say, i am very, very surprised. Pleasantly. The game looks NOTHING like when it first released, and with the new update, so many things were added, and now the game has actual depth. I am having fun playing No Man's Sky. I never thought i could say that without punching myself in the face, or lying to myself because i didn't want $60 to go to waste. And finally, the games has functional multiplayer (i didn't play it very much yet, but i encountered no bug up until now, but don't take my word for that.). If Hello Games keeps this game alive with those kind of updates, i can see this game becoming an actual great financial success. This time, without lying to us, the playerbase.

Now, for something very important:
Should Hello Games be forgiven?
No. We should accept what happened and support Hello Games in the future, BUT: do you remember how lootboxes started out? It only takes one successful example of something before others want to try it, too. The game, as of today, is just worlds better than the original version. And if i pay $60, i want my money's worth, and people who buy it today get a better product for half the prize. That is just bullshit, but if those updates keep coming, i'll gladly say that my $60 were well spent. However, this is probably the best example for "games as a service". And this is why we all should move on from the release, while still keeping the release in mind, and support Hello Games as a playerbase-focused company, who did NOT just take our money and run, but actually cared about their community.

So, in conclusion:
Congratulations, Hello Games, for one of the biggest and well-deserved comebacks in recent history, and i'm looking forward to what else you have in mind.
And please add sandworms.

Reviews.169330:
blah bla, ultimate redemption story, I'm sure everyone knows by now.  

The game in it's current state is a must experience absolute masterpiece, particularly if you are into interesting (and at times trippy) experiences, and particularly in VR.  The downside to VR is that the graphically fidelity is so great in regular mode that it is a shame how fuzzy everything becomes in VR since it simply cannot manage the same level of detail.  Basically, it looks good in VR, but by comparison to the amazing looking regular mode (assuming you can play on 4k or at least 1080p) it is a let down.  This is not their fault, just hardware limitations right now.  

I have never played a better sandbox game ever and I have never played a more visually stunning game ever.  It is hands down the most beautiful game ever made.  There are games with technically better graphics out there, but not much better, and this is not about realism, but about fantastical sights.  

Environments are extremely immersive, with so much going on around you, so much attention to detail.  It is amazing that they have managed this achievement using procedural generation. 

There is so much content and so much to do that you can get lost in the game for ages.  It really gives you that hard to achieve feeling of exploration in an infinite environment.

I am leaving this as a positive review (I have reviewed it before and this is an update/edit) because it is such an amazing and unique experience that you must try, but the caveat is that I don't actually play it much at all and haven't for ages because I burned out on it years ago.  It is a real shame because they have added so much, but none of it really expands the core gameplay loop.  I really wish the game was in its current state when I first poured 200 hours into it (my account says less, but I originally "borrowed" it), as it would have really enhanced the experience.  

So for new players, you really need to experience this and it is the best time to hop in and try it - I absolutely recommend, it is a treat.  For those who have already played it a bunch, I really cannot recommend it as there is really nothing new for you.  I always hop on and give it a go after updates just to check it out again and marvel at the visual additions, but the novelty wears off quickly as there is nothing meaty to sink your teeth into, no compelling gameplay to keep you entertained.  I know some people who have played many hundreds more hours than me still enjoy it as they just love experiencing this world forever and somehow do not get bored, but for people who need a good underlying game with their amazing experiences, you will not find it here after playing it for 10 hours, 30 hours, 100 hours, however long it takes you to get bored with the endless sandbox without a real game contained within.  The original excitement with this was fantastic, and again, I wish I got to experience that in the game's current state because that would have been amazing, but once you've already done it you really can't experience it again as the sense of wonder and excitement is gone.  You don't know exactly what is on the other side of that portal, but in a sense you do, so the magic is gone.

How would I fix this?  Well I am not sure there is anything to fix.  They tried hard to fill the game with tasky type stuff to do so that it feels like there is a purpose, but none of that was any good, this game is and has always been more about the experience of exploring a wonderous and exotic universe.  It would be out of place to throw in pvp firefights or something just to give the gameplay some meat, although in some ways I kinda wish they would at this point because then at least more people might get to experience this amazing looking game.  Personally I wish that there was some kind of infinite puzzler here.  Something like The Witness, so that while I'm exploring this cool universe for its own sake, I'm also driven to keep playing by some intriguing gameplay, even it is just one more puzzle to solve.  I've put more hours into games like Gemcraft because while they do not look great, there is a challenge there, something to try to achieve.  The union of a game like NMS and a really good puzzler with hundreds and hundreds of levels that ultimately tell a story (a la Johnathan Blow style) would be an ultimate gaming experience for me.  

NMS really fell short with building in an intriguing mystery to uncover as you explore.  For the first many hours I always felt like I was on the verge of discovering something, of unlocking some amazing never before seen thing, the mysteries of the universe or something like that, and being the only one to have done it, and it was great.  It gave the feeling but the payload never comes.  The feeling itself is worth it but I cannot see how anybody could not be at least somewhat disappointed that it doesn't seem to follow through.  That said, this seems to be a perception of what the game was originally trying to achieve that only some of us in the NMS community have, while other players have approached the game differently, more like a Minecraft in space of sorts, and they seem to enjoy it for that.

Introduction: So I want to tell you a story of two companies, lets call them HG and EA.  Both release a product the population is insanely excited about, both release to millions of units sold, both fall short due to over-promising or flat out false promotion.

Public Response: We unite as gamers, and viciously attack both of these companies.  They both issue apologies, roll out a future release schedule, and promise that all of the things they said will be in the game, WILL be in the game.  They both beg our patience, the best is yet to come.  Now we as gamers went on with our lives, because that's how it works.  We get hyped, and we get let down.  We are used to it.

The follow through: Here is where our two companies diverge.  EA within 3 weeks of release cuts the development team by 90%, reassigns the lead devs as well as anyone capable of making any change to the game, and cancels the games roll out 15 months later after, to a collective sign from the gaming community.  HG however hires dozens of designers and programmers, communicates with their gamer base, and not only meets the roll-out schedule but does it for free!  They pour millions into the game, turning it from a stale saltine cracker of a launch to something halfway decent.  They then keep going, content patch after content patch.  They start winning awards, they change minds, they turn a defeat into a victory.

They keep going, from base building to fleet building, a horror patch where you clear derelict and possibly haunted freighters, new ships (some even living), cleaner planets, deep sea overhauls, base building (even under the sea) random space encounters, multi-player, mech suits, almost a dozen economy patches to keep it fun, cosmetics, pets, quality of life, sand worms, you name it.

Your money is a method of encouragement or damnation.  Put money into something, you tell the market this is what we want (or are at least OK with).  We are gamers, to say we are familiar with disappointing launches is an understatement.  I ask you this though, how many times has a company even met your expectations as far as supporting a game after launch. HG (Hello Games) has set the standard for that, exceeding every expectation, and continues to push forward.

So you may still hold a grudge to what HG released years ago, maybe all companies should get it perfect on the first try every time.  Reality however has shown us that game development can be more than a little messy.  All I ask is this, which behavior do you want to support, the cut and run EA style leaving you with a half done product and getting out because there is more money to be made with another release, or the HG style where they stay with you for the long haul.

I will buy anything HG puts out, this is what we should expect from our developers.
